en: Preface to the Commentary on the Song of Realizing the Way by Chan Master Zhuyuan:

When Shen Guang saw Bodhidharma, he prostrated three times, stood up, and was entrusted with the robe and the Dharma. When Zhenjue visited Caoxi, he circled the meditation seat, shook his staff, and thereby established the fundamental tenets.
Indeed, the subtle and profound essence of the mind-Dharma transcends the reach of words; so it was with the various patriarchs who followed.

They practiced the striking of staffs and the shouting of "Ho," rolled balls, and performed dances; they beat drums and shook bells, using great mechanisms and great functions to manifest the wondrous art of benefiting both self and others.
Thus it was said that in this eastern land there were those of great Mahayana capacity who transmitted the Buddha-mind lineage.
This is precisely what is meant. Only Bodhisattvas of the Mahāyāna can act for both themselves and others; Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas cannot.
Thus we know that the transmission of our school is no trivial matter. Lately, monastic communities have not followed the ancient tradition;
some may possess a degree of insight but lack true practice, thereby losing the essence of the Way. Others may possess skill in meditative stillness but are unable...
To proclaim the essential tenets for the sake of benefiting sentient beings and engaging with others, yet lose their practical application—this is what has occurred.

If one were to possess both essence and function, and be fully equipped in both practice and realization, there was only Master Zhuyuan in the regions between the Yangtze and Huai rivers. This master had early on traveled extensively to consult renowned elders;

there were no scriptures of the Buddhas and Patriarchs that he did not investigate deeply. Yet, he stood out preeminently by taking the Great Matter as his personal responsibility. At the end of his life, he met [Master] Wuxue...
Nengjiao Gong’s spiritual capacity and words were in perfect accord with [the Master’s], and he subsequently inherited his Dharma. He resided twice at Miaoguo Temple in Po.
Becoming weary of worldly entanglements, he retired to Nan-chao. Scholars from throughout the realm flocked to him in great numbers until there was no room left in his quarters.

When someone requested a commentary on the *Zhenjue zhengdao ge* (Song of Realizing the Path through True Awakening), the Master analyzed it point by point in response to questions; the scholars recorded these explanations, which formed a complete volume. Chen Shan of Gushu...

He wished to carve [this work] into printing blocks to benefit future students and requested a preface from me. I say that while the awakening to principle (*li*) is one, the cultivation of phenomena (*shi*) is inexhaustible.

Thus, the Huayan teaching of the four dharma-realms culminates in the "non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena" (*shishi wuai*), meaning that not a single dharma is abandoned and not a single thing fails to attain its proper place. True Awakening began from...

Regarding the practice of contemplation according to the teachings: it is like a person who has already made his fields, gardens, and dwelling prosperous; yet, although he possesses a special deed of conveyance, it has not been formally validated.
Upon meeting the Sixth Patriarch, he was like one presenting that deed to the authorities, where a single seal is affixed to finalize it, ensuring the family estate is preserved forever.
His teachings accorded with those of Mazu, Baizhang, Huangbo, Linji, Nanyang, and Dazhu, and it was from him that they all derived their methods of expounding the sutras.
How could a fledgling practitioner like I presume to speak of this?

Furthermore, I have heard that although Master Wuneng was proficient in the Buddhist scriptures as well as the teachings of Confucius, Laozi, and the hundred schools of thought, the Master surpassed him in erudition and eloquence; thus, he was able to fully unfold the treasury of true awakening.

These are merely matters for special entertainment. As for those who, within the meditation hall, interrogate with mechanisms as swift as lightning and reveal the ultimate core of the patch-robed monks—when encountering such masters, one must present them separately.
Written in the eighth month of autumn in the sixth year of Zhizheng (the Gengchen year), by the monk Daxin of Longxiang,
in homage to the Song Verses on the Realization of the Way by the Great Master Zhenjue of Yongjia,
with the commentary of Chan Master Fahui Hongde at the Zhuyuan Hermitage in Nanchao.
Compiled by the disciple of the Way, Dehong. Have you not seen?
(The very first stroke is presented face-to-face; it is also said: "Where has he gone?
The man of the Way who is beyond study and non-action (is originally right here). He does not eliminate delusive thoughts, nor does he seek the Truth. (For now...)
Faith (half of it). The true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature (vaguely like crossing the state of Yue).
The illusory and empty body is itself the Dharma-body (resembling Yangzhou). The Dharma-body is awakened and realizes there is not a single thing (to call it a "thing" is immediately incorrect).
The original source and fundamental nature is the natural, celestial Buddha (I do not care to hear the word "Buddha"). The five aggregates are floating...
Clouds come and go across the sky (a mound of earth rising from level ground). The bubbles of the three poisons emerge and submerge in vain (counting bones within empty space).
The scholar who has severed [learning] has nothing to learn. When there is nothing to learn, learning is severed. To do nothing is to act.

There is nothing to be done. To act with nothing to be done is to act where there is nothing. This is not merely the world-transcending non-action of the "extreme learning" (jue-xue) found in the secular world;
rather, it is the ultimate non-action that transcends both the mundane and the supramundane.

That which is the perfection of self-awakening, awakening others, and the fulfillment of awakened practice—the manifestation of the three bodies and the full display of the ten titles—is the ultimate non-action of all Buddhas. [The stages of] the Ten Sages, the Three Worthies, and the Six...
"Completing the myriad practices and attaining bodhi only after all sentient beings have been delivered" refers to the non-action of the ultimate study of the Bodhisattva.

"Severing the defilements of the three realms, transcending the birth-and-death of segmented existence, exhausting all outflows, and not undergoing further existence" refers to the non-action of the ultimate study of the Two Vehicles.
To penetrate and awaken to the heart-source of all Buddhas and to thoroughly master the "nose-ring" of the patch-robed monk—this is [the practice of]... cultivation.
The "Eye of Wisdom Perfectly Bright through Correspondence with Understanding" is the absolute learning and non-action of the patched-robed monk (*śramaṇa*).
The three periods of time are equal, and the single path is pure and void. The entire world of the ten directions is the whole body of this śramaṇa;
the myriad phenomena and all that exists are the adamantine true essence. It is indestructible and unmixed, without deficiency and without excess. Above, there are no Buddhas to be realized.
Below, there are no sentient beings to be saved. All is level and settled; all is spacious and open. Body and mind are as one, with nothing remaining outside the self.
One may be called a man of the Way who has transcended study and is non-active. Reaching this state, there is no second person, nor is there a second thought.
The sentiments of sage and ordinary being have vanished; the views of truth and falsehood are empty. Looking back, even ignorance is seen as real.
Nature is itself Buddha-nature. This illusory, empty body is itself the Dharma-body. Vastly encompassing, it has no exterior; minutely penetrating, it has no interior.
It is boundlessly non-active, spontaneously transforming in stillness. Without name or character, without going or coming, it remains eternally and serenely constant from antiquity to the present.
Therefore it is said: "The Dharma-body is fully awakened and realizes there is not a single thing; its original source and self-nature are celestial and true."
The Buddha thoroughly understood that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the three poisons (*tri-doṣa*) are like floating clouds, bubbles on water, or empty appearances and disappearances.

The five aggregates are form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; the three poisons are greed, hatred, and delusion. Furthermore, it is said they are the realms of hungry ghosts, animals, and hell-beings.

Nevertheless, these are merely matters at the periphery of the vehicles of teaching (*śāsana-yāna*); in the school of Linji, one is still only halfway there. Only upon arriving home is one truly at rest.
How can you express it in a single phrase? Do you not see?
For his sake, I have opened a single thread: red dust rises from the bottom of the well; white silk is spun upon the mountain peak.
A cubit-and-two-inch beard grows beneath the chin; an octagonal millstone turns in the empty sky.
Realizing the true mark (empty space eating an iron staff). The non-existence of persons and dharmas (Siddhārtha born in the royal palace).
Instantaneously extinguishing the karma of Avīci (from where did you get this news?). If one uses false speech to deceive sentient beings (what such desperate urgency!).
One will personally invite the severing of one's tongue for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges (the deep forest hides fierce tigers; the shallow grass reveals swarms of snakes).
The single characteristic that is without characteristics is called the true characteristic (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). This is precisely the inherently existing awakened mind of all sentient beings.
From immeasurable kalpas past until this very day, this mind has been fundamentally pure, fundamentally complete, fundamentally endowed with all, and fundamentally wondrous.
Vast as the great void and bright as the clear moon, it is equal to those of the three periods of time.

The Buddhas are of one essence and without distinction. This is truly because when the two polarities first divided and the three powers (the human, earth, and heaven) began to be established, sentient beings initially lacked awakening and relied upon consciousness to undergo birth.
They were blind to the eye of wisdom in the dim alleys of existence, crawling within the nine abodes;

they locked true awakening away in the night of dreams, remaining mired in the midst of the triple world. Only through the instruction of a teacher did they finally awaken to their former errors, turning the light back upon themselves to penetrate [reality].
Having penetrated the true source, one is said to have realized this stage where there is no person and no dharma, no Buddha and no sentient beings, no going and no coming, and no birth and no death.
The karmic consciousness of ignorance accumulated over vast eons is instantly dissolved in a single thought-moment; thus it is said:
"In a single *kṣaṇa*, the karma of Avīci is extinguished. *Avīci* is a Sanskrit term meaning "uninterrupted," referring to the realm of ultimate suffering.
This is a matter of the prison. Yongjia feared that people of the world would not be able to believe it; therefore, he made a vow, saying:
"If I were to deceive others with these words, may I myself undergo the punishment of having my tongue pulled out for as many kalpas as there are motes of dust.
This was possible because of his profound compassion and poignant pity. A *kalpa* refers to a period of time. Can you still believe this? Listen further to a verse:
Realizing the true mark: there is neither person nor dharma. The wild weeds of ignorance are uprooted from their very foundations;
the ocean of three thousand worlds is cold and silent. All sages and worthies are left speechless.
To suddenly awaken and realize it—this is still the work of a dull-witted fellow. As for the Tathāgata-dhyāna—who would bestow such a name?
The essence of the six perfections and myriad practices is perfectly complete; one may know this as proper etiquette (though others say it is like painting legs on a snake).
Within the dream, the six realms of existence are clearly manifest; yet upon awakening, all is empty, with not even a great chiliocosm remaining. (This is still a bit short of the mark.)

Sudden awakening is not realized through gradual expedients; rather, it is for those of superior faculties and sharp intelligence who attain a thousand awakenings upon hearing once and achieve a hundredfold certainty upon understanding once.
It is like cutting a single strand of silk: when one is cut, all are cut; when one is realized, all are realized.

"Tathāgata-dhyāna" (the meditation of the Thus-Come One) is the meaning of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena; that which comes has nowhere from which it comes. It is not the four dhyānas or the eight [liberations].
The Chan of Samādhi is precisely the Chan of Master Bodhidharma—the direct transmission of the Tathāgata’s mind-seal without relying on words or letters.
Once this mind is realized, all conditions are relinquished; this is the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).
Being originally pure is the perfection of precept (*śīla-pāramitā*). Not rejoicing in praise and not feeling anger at slander is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).

It is the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*). To be without delusion in every thought-moment is the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*). To be inwardly tranquil and unwavering is the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).
For wisdom’s illumination to be like the sun is the perfection of insight (*prajñā-pāramitā*).

Upon reaching this stage, the three thousand majestic deportments and eighty thousand subtle practices are, step by step, all in accord with reality (*tathatā*); there is not a single principle that is not perfected, nor a single matter that is not so.

Because they are not so prepared, it is said that the essence of the six perfections and myriad practices is perfect and complete. When deluded, all objective realms are likewise thus; after awakening, the myriad dharmas all cease. Therefore it is said:
"Within the dream, clearly there are the six destinies; upon waking, everything is empty—there is not even a Great Thousandfold World.
As for the "Great Thousandfold World," this refers to the transformed realm of Śākyamuni Tathāgata. If even the transformed realm is empty, how much more so the six destinies?
As for that one phrase after awakening—how do you speak of it?
Sudden awakening is the Tathāgata-dhyāna; shattering empty space, there are no two sides. A single expanse of brilliance cannot be concealed;
it is clearly and uniquely revealed before the kalpa.
No sin or merit (the wind cannot blow in). No loss or gain (the rain cannot wet it).

Within the nature of quiescent extinction, do not seek or inquire (when the sky clears, the sun shines as before). For some time now, the dusty mirror has never been polished (raising weapons on level ground).
Today, you must clearly analyze and discern this (try to bring it forth and see). Who is without thought? (A flash of lightning in the void.)
A flash of lightning. Who is unborn? (An iron serpent lies across the ancient path. If one is unborn, there is no non-birth. (One will follow the talisman as it moves.
Summon the wooden man with its mechanical joints and ask him. (Brandish the staff and strike! Seeking the Buddha’s grace for merit—when will it ever be accomplished?
(A second offense will not be tolerated.)
The nature of my mind is fundamentally empty; sin and merit have no master. Since sin and merit have no master, how could there be any harm or benefit?
Body and mind are quiescent, equal, and of one suchness. They are free from the marks of words, free from the marks of conceptual deliberation, free from all thoughts, and free from all attachments.
Therefore, it is said: "Do not seek by questioning. The Great Master, out of compassion for those who come to study, extended his own realization to others. This is truly so.

Due to this toil, one gives rise to self-confidence that one is incapable [of awakening]. One turns one's back on enlightenment and unites with the sensory dusts, abandoning the root to pursue the branches.

Drifting and wandering along with karma, one strays so far as to forget the way back. Enveloped by the habitual tendencies of views, hearing, cognition, and affectionate attachment, one’s own true nature cannot manifest before oneself.
The spiritual powers and radiant light must not be revealed prematurely; it is like an ancient mirror long buried in dust and grime, unable to reflect objects.
Therefore, today I shall clearly dissect and analyze for you: where is there a "Maitreya born of heaven" or a "Śākyamuni existing naturally"?
Thus it is said: "Who is without thought? Who is without birth? If you can believe this, apply yourself with utmost diligence and break through [the barriers].
This is one's own precious treasury. To see through to one’s original face, the inner mind and outer objects become vast, empty, and harmoniously fused.

Thus, the holy and the ordinary are equally transcended; hence it is said: "If there is no birth, there is no non-birth. Livelihood, production, and industry are all in no way contrary to the true mark (*dharmatā*).
Furthermore, this Dharma abides in its own place, and the characteristics of the world are eternally constant. Yet, there is also concern for the world...
People, based on the view that there is no arising or ceasing through non-thought, claim for themselves that they have "hundredfold completion and thousandfold resolution.
This is like a wooden puppet operated by a mechanism; it has no mind or thought. To seek Buddhahood while in such a state is impossible. Therefore, it is said: "When will you ever achieve it?"
This is precisely when it is accomplished.
There is neither sin nor merit; there is neither loss nor gain. A single phrase, clearly realized, transcends ten billion worlds. Night after night, the moon sinks toward the west;
day after day, the sun rises from the east.
Release the four great elements (cease your fabrication of the strange). Do not try to grasp them (it is all error).

Within the nature of quiescent extinction, follow what is offered for drink and food (a single horn on a five-colored qilin). All conditioned phenomena are impermanent and entirely empty (will you weep when your father dies?).
This is precisely the Tathāgata’s Great Perfect Enlightenment (the stars fall from the bright day and clear sky).
If one clings to them, one loses the proper measure and inevitably enters a deviant path; if one lets them be natural, the body has neither going nor staying.
One who has reached the bottom knows that the four great elements are fundamentally empty and the five aggregates do not exist. They stand tall and majestic, solitary and remote;
free and at ease, without restraint or bondage. Their expansive openness is like the great void; their purity is like the bright moon by the water’s edge or the forest.

Below, one wanders freely as one pleases. With coarse food and simple clothing, one drinks and eats according to conditions. One turns back to observe that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent and that all dharmas are originally empty and quiescent.
To know thus, to see thus, and to believe and understand thus—such that no marks of dharmas arise—is the Great Perfect Enlightenment of the Tathāgata.
Release the four great elements; do not grasp them. Amidst a blazing conflagration, how could a mosquito find a place to alight?
One staff is supported by two people; across ten thousand miles of empty space, a solitary falcon soars.
To speak with certainty: (a single flake of snow flying into the flaming heavens). To represent a true monk: (the nose straight, the eyes slanted).

If someone is unwilling to accept this, how can they investigate it according to their own whims? (How could they possibly do so? Directly cutting through to the root is what the Buddhas have certified; plucking leaves and seeking branches—I am not capable of that.
(I simply cannot bring myself to analyze it in such a way.)

His wisdom-mirror is perfectly clear and bright, such that beauty and ugliness appear of themselves. Whether right or wrong, whether deviant or correct, his single word is definitive and never subject to alternative interpretation.
Internally he harbors the practices of a Bodhisattva; externally he manifests the body of a Śrāvaka, acting as the leader of humans and devas.
He is the compassionate vessel for those in the sea of suffering; therefore, he is called a monk who manifests the truth.
Yet there may be those with perverse interpretations and heterodox views who, lacking faith and acceptance in their hearts, arbitrarily pose questions according to their own whims.

Even if all the grasses, trees, forests, rice, hemp, bamboos, and reeds were transformed into tongues, and each of those tongues were to raise the aforementioned challenges and difficulties, they would not last for even the snap of a finger before being utterly extinguished.
Responding universally to high and low, there is no discrepancy between before and after. Thus it is said: "Directly cutting through to the root is what the Buddhas have certified;
picking leaves and seeking branches is not for me.
This is the definitive teaching that manifests the true Sangha: Caoxi, the Sixth Patriarch, Neng of Lingnan, who followed Master Ma.
After the turmoil, the blazing flames continue to link the fragrant blossoms, inheriting the ancestral lamp.
The *maṇi* jewel (one lift, forty-nine counts)—people do not recognize it (they have missed it). Within the *tathāgatagarbha*, one has personally obtained it (it was originally right here).

The six kinds of divine functions, empty yet not empty (the silver mountains...)* *Note: The final phrase "銀山只" (yínshānzhǐ) appears to be an incomplete fragment of a larger verse or commentary, likely referring to the "silver mountains and iron walls" (*yínhuán tiěbiàn*) that represent the vast, impenetrable nature of reality.*
This is the Silver Mountain). A single orb of light is neither form nor non-form (the iron wall is simply an iron wall).
In Sanskrit it is *maṇi*; in the Tang language it is translated as "Wish-Fulfilling" (*cintāmaṇi*). It is also said to be the heart-jewel of the King of the Golden-Winged Birds (*garuḍa*).
Within the human dimension, it is precisely one's own inherently possessed nature of numinous clarity and true awakening. All supernatural powers and samādhis [arise from this].

It is inherently complete from the beginning; it is only because of the weariness of worldly existence that one lacks self-confidence. Turning one's back on awakening and uniting with the dust of sensory objects, one is deluded and does not know this for oneself;
hence it is said, "People do not recognize it. Only the Buddhas and Tathāgatas possess a wondrous nature that is perfectly luminous, profoundly still, and empty-quiescent.
From within it, hundreds of thousands of samādhis manifest at will; hence it is said, "Within the Tathāgata-garbha, one personally recovers this maṇi jewel."

It can respond to the five colors; some say it has six apertures. This is a metaphor for how the human being is originally a single, pure brilliance, which divides into six to form a harmonious union.
Once a single faculty returns to its source, the functions of the other six become quiescent. Thus it is said: "The sixfold divine functions are both empty and not empty;
this single sphere of light is neither color nor non-color."

The mani-jewel: people do not recognize it; though its brilliance is vivid and clear, it appears black as lacquer. The myriad phenomena of the universe are all contained within and harmonized therein;
from this, the four classes of sages and the six realms of ordinary beings emerge.

Purifying the five eyes (the eastern house lights its lamp), attaining the five powers (the western house sits in darkness). Only through realization can one know that it is difficult to fathom (when people are level they do not speak;
when water is level it does not flow). Looking at one’s form in a mirror is not difficult to see (one must strictly avoid touching it);
grasping for the moon in the water—how could anyone pick it up? (You are but a fellow who plays with shadows and light.)

As for the five eyes: the celestial eye perceives all things with penetration; the fleshly eye is not deluded by external objects; the dharma-eye perceives that the nature of phenomena is fundamentally empty;
the wisdom-eye illuminates with intelligence, seeing through to clarity; and the Buddha-eye regards all things as equal.

Once these five eyes are purified, the power of faith, the power of diligence, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom will spontaneously manifest before one. The Dharma-gate of the mind-ground can only be known through personal realization.

This is not something that can be fathomed by ordinary sentiments. If a person turns their light back upon themselves and perceives their original face through to the very core, it will not be difficult.
However, if one falsely identifies the shadows and reflections of external objects as oneself, it is like a monkey grasping at the moon in the water—how could one ever seize it?
Therefore, it is said: "To see one's form in a mirror is not difficult; to grasp the moon in the water is another matter."
Who can grasp it?
Purify the five eyes; attain the five powers. Squeezing juice from the head of a scale-weight—what a perfectly whole gate of liberation!
It is flung wide open, yet none can enter.
Always walking alone (the two eyebrows above the eyes are horizontal); always treading alone (the path beneath the feet reaches the heavens).

Those who have attained enlightenment travel together on the road to Nirvana (but where, for now, does the head of that road lie?). With ancient airs and pure spirit, one’s wind naturally rises high (Venerable Yunju);
with a haggard countenance and sturdy bones, others pay no heed (only then will there be a slight degree of correspondence).
Master Pang asked Mazu, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as his companion?
Mazu replied, "When you can drink up all the waters of the West River in a single gulp, I will tell you.
If one can see through to the bottom here, one may then stride freely across the sea and walk alone upon the crimson clouds; one will then walk hand-in-hand with the patriarchs of old.
This is beyond the ordinary. It is just like when a monk asked Qianfeng, "The Buddhas of the ten directions all enter the single path to Nirvana;
where exactly does that path begin? Qianfeng took his staff, drew a line, and said, "It is right here. But how about this? Therefore it is said:
"His demeanor is ancient and his spirit is pure, his wind naturally lofty; his appearance is haggard and his bones are firm, yet people pay him no heed."
Whether or not someone will attain enlightenment thirty years from now remains uncertain.
He always walks alone; he always strides forth alone. The tiger-like sandals upon his feet turn back and sweep across the vast void;
unaware, he has trampled the path by which he came.
The destitute Śākya son (the master of the house) claims with his own mouth that he is poor (be alert!).

In truth, it is his body that is poor, but his Way is not poor (at another time, on another day, do not let yourself be deceived). Being poor, his body constantly wears coarse hempen cloth (the left eye is half a catty).
The Way is the heart-treasury, a priceless jewel (eight *liang* in the right eye). A priceless jewel (a repeated phrase meaning it should not be consumed).

Its use is inexhaustible (if it had an end, what else could it serve for?). Benefiting beings according to conditions, one never begrudges them (who does not possess this? even the ground beneath one’s sitting mat).
The three bodies and four wisdoms are perfectly complete within its essence (the "partial" aspect within the "central"). The eight liberations...

The Seal of the Mind-Ground of the Six Supernormal Powers (centered within the partial). When the superior person makes a single resolution, all is understood (originally not increased by so much as a hair’s breadth).
Those of middling and inferior capacity hear much yet have little faith (nor is it diminished by so much as a hair’s breadth).
One simply unties the soiled garment from within one’s own breast (cultivation and realization are not non-existent). Who can boast of their diligence toward the external (defilement is not...)?
[It is] attained). An ancient said: "In studying the Way, one must first learn poverty; once poverty is learned, the Way will become intimate.

This precept [forbids] greed and other such traits, as well as external ornamentation. Those who have left the household life take the clan-name of the Buddha, and are thus called Śākyaputras. "Putra" (son) refers to a male.
This is a general designation. In the Sanskrit language it is *Śākya*, which here means "Capable Benevolence" (*Néng rén*). To omit saying "Śākya" is for the sake of brevity.
Having nothing external to his person while harboring the holy Way within his mind, he is truly not poor.

Furthermore, to say he is "poor" refers to one who constantly wears coarse, threadbare garments while the Way—meaning a priceless treasure—is stored within the heart; thus, the hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates and immeasurable subtle meanings are ever-present.
They are fully endowed with the merit of the sands [of the Ganges], the samādhis, and the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Their manifestations are inexhaustible and their applications are endless.
They receive beings and benefit living things, administering medicine according to the illness. With great joy and great renunciation, they are without stinginess or regret.

They transform the eight consciousnesses into the four wisdoms and consolidate the four wisdoms into the three bodies (*trikāya*). Even down to the eight liberations, the six supernormal powers, and the myriad phenomena of the universe—all are sealed by the single seal.
It is fixed without the slightest deviation; thus it is said that within the essence lies the Seal of the Perfect Heart-ground (*citta-bhūmi*).

Those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom resolve all at once and comprehend all at once. Those of middling or inferior capacity encounter obstructions wherever they turn, and for this reason, despite their extensive learning, they possess little faith.
One who has reached the bottom simply uses the state of correct awakening to illuminate themselves with spiritual clarity.
One washes and polishes away the subtle habitual stains accumulated over immeasurable kalpas. Like frost and dew upon ripening fruit, they emerge as soon as one turns the head;

like moonlight on a turbulent rapids, where thousands of waves and myriad billows touch it yet cannot disperse it, one finally ceases to be deluded by the māras of birth-and-death and the five aggregates.
Thus it is said: "Only within one's own breast does one untie the soiled garment; who can boast of their diligence toward the external? This is because...
This is not like those who run outward in pursuit.
The destitute Śākya son declares himself poor, yet whatever he picks up with his hands, he uses with intimacy: the golden bird beneath the water is the sun in the sky;
the child within the eye is the person before one’s face.
Let others slander him (a clay figure eating an iron staff); let others be wrong (fish eyes mixed with bright pearls).
To set fire to the heavens merely exhausts oneself (punishing the one who accuses another for the very crime they committed).
When I hear this, it is as if drinking nectar (one has already fallen into their trap). It melts away and suddenly enters the inconceivable (half the work is saved).
Contemplating harsh words (gold does not trade with gold), one realizes these are merits (water does not wash water).
This constitutes my true spiritual friend (the "Shang Daren Qiu Yiji" inscription).

Without resentment toward slander or attachment to kinship (the overlapping mountain passes), what could better manifest the power of non-arising compassion and patience (a single arrow piercing the azure sky)?
When the mind corresponds with emptiness, what cause is there for sorrow or joy regarding praise or blame?

When the body corresponds with emptiness, what cause is there for suffering or pleasure when it is cut by a blade or smeared with incense? When one's means of livelihood correspond with emptiness, what gain or loss is there in giving, seizing, or taking?
Therefore, those on the Path do not compete with things over right and wrong; when opposition or favor comes before them, they are as if they did not hear it.
I do not see it. His skillful means are finite, while my non-acceptance is infinite. It is like a person holding a torch to burn the heavens;
he merely exhausts himself, for what effect can there be upon the heavens? Upon hearing this, it was as if drinking nectar, and my mind became naturally cool and serene.
One enters instantaneously into the inconceivable realm of liberation. Looking back upon these evil words, one sees that they are all merits.
This is because the nature of speech is empty and enemies and kin are equal; thus, they become my spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
It is just as the Buddhas of the past were, in every life and birth throughout kalpas, harmed and vexed by Devadatta in every place, yet through their compassion...
The power of patience brings about the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; therefore, it is said that one does not give rise to enmity or intimacy because of slander.
What does this signify? It signifies the power of non-arising compassion and patience.

When faced with the slanders of others, leave their faults as they are; immediately turn back and observe: "Who is this other? Whether they possess extraordinary features or inferior forms, all are...
This is an illusion. All names and noble titles are collectively empty.
The fundamental principle (zōng) is pervasive; the teaching (shuō) is also pervasive. With concentration and wisdom perfectly bright, one does not stagnate in emptiness.
It is not that I alone have attained this realization; the essence of all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is identical.

The "Patriarchal Penetration" (*zongtong*) refers to awakening to the essential heart-mind of all Buddhas. It is the path of the Great Master Bodhidharma’s direct transmission of pointing directly at [the nature of mind].
It cannot be known through intellectual wisdom (*jñāna*), nor can it be cognized by consciousness (*vijñāna*).

It exists solely in the individual’s own realization and awakening, reaching the ground where there is neither realization nor awakening. For this reason, the successive patriarchs of old have appeared one after another, directing [beings] toward the thousand sages.

To hold fast to the crown of the head is the single transmission; it enables the student to fully attain the wondrous method of direct pointing, which is called the "thoroughness of the school" (zongtong).

Thereafter, one is entrusted with the key to the treasury to peruse the holy teachings of a lifetime, so as to fully know the methods of the sudden, gradual, secret, and indefinite, as well as the flavors of the *zang*, *tong*, *bie*, and *yuan* [teachings].
This is called the "thoroughness of the exposition" (shuotong). Thus, there is the thoroughness of the school and the thoroughness of the exposition.

Once they have been mastered, when concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are equalized, one may truly be said to possess perfect illumination (*yuanming*) that does not stagnate in emptiness. Yongjia himself said:

"It is not only I who alone have now attained a thorough understanding of this principle of the perfect illumination of concentration and wisdom; I have realized this same essence together with all the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
This is what the ancients meant when they said: "In the world there are no two paths; among sages there are no two minds. As for "the sands of the Ganges," it refers to the West...
The heavens contain rivers as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, each forty li in width. Within these rivers, there is sand as fine as flour.
The World-Honored One, when preaching the Dharma, frequently used these sands as metaphors. Now, Yongjia speaks in accordance with the scriptures.
The fundamental principle is pervasive; the teaching is pervasive. A bright sun shines in a cloudless sky.
The myriad meanings of hundreds of thousands of samādhis reside solely within the ordinary activities of daily life.
The Lion’s Roar (the void opens its great mouth); speaking without fear (ten thousand apertures turned by a single tongue).
When the hundred beasts hear it, their brains all split (a flake of snow flying upon the flames of a red furnace). The fragrant elephant rushes about, losing his majesty (it is not his realm).
The devas and nāgas listen in silence, giving rise to joy (still carrying traces of consciousness).
The lion is the king among beasts; if it lets out a single roar, all other animals hear it and their brains are split asunder.

This serves as a metaphor for the perfect and sudden Dharma-sound proclaimed by Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas, which causes the palaces of Māra to tremble, while those of the Hīnayāna and non-Buddhists each give rise to doubt and fail to comprehend it.
It is like those with eyes who could not see the Śāla trees at the assembly of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
That body has ears but does not hear the Perfect and Sudden Teaching; it is like those who withdrew from their seats during the assembly at the Lotus Sutra.

Therefore it is said: "The path beyond the ordinary is not transmitted by the thousand sages; students weary their bodies like monkeys grasping at shadows. Thus it says: "The fragrant elephant rushes about, losing its majesty.
The "fragrant elephant" is a metaphor for the Bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings and the various followers of the Two Vehicles. Although...

Having realized the principle of the emptiness of phenomena, yet not clearly understanding the capacity for the Perfect and Sudden teaching, they are like fragrant elephants who, despite their majesty and virtue, lose their courage and flee upon hearing the roar of the lion.
Only the devas and nāga kings, whose past熏習 (karmic perfuming) consists of great seeds, experience universal joy upon hearing the perfect sound;
thus it is said that "listening in stillness gives rise to delight."
The Lion’s Roar is preached fearlessly; Gavāmpati bites his tongue; the Sea God, in a rage, seizes his coral whip;
and King Sumeru suffers pain that pierces to the core.
Wandering through rivers and seas (Why roam about in such disorder?), Traversing mountains and streams (Return me the price for my straw sandals!).

Seeking masters and visiting paths to practice Zen (Who is lacking anything?), Since I have recognized the road to Caoxi (Try picking it up and looking at it), I have come to know that birth and death are not mutually involved (Night travel is forbidden; you must arrive by dawn).

In ancient times, when venerable masters left one monastic community to enter another and sought out spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), it was all for the sake of resolving the great matter of their own person.

This was like Sudhana’s fifty-three pilgrimages, Xuefeng’s three ascents and nine arrivals, and even the way the old monks of the world traveled to the doors of various spiritual friends before finally reaching the stage of non-doubt. Thus, Zhengjue said of himself:
He went to Caoxi to receive the Sixth Patriarch’s seal of approval on the Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground, thereby realizing that birth and death do not interfere with one another.
Wandering through rivers and seas, traversing mountains and streams, he sought a single coin from everyone he met.
"How wonderful was that simple-minded Baguai of Kaizhou! At the crossroads, he acted with unrestrained madness."
Walking is also Chan; sitting is also Chan. Whether speaking or silent, moving or still, the body is ever at ease.
Even if one encounters a sharp blade, one remains ever composed; even if one encounters poison, one remains ever tranquil.
My Master met the Buddha Dīpaṃkara; for many kalpas he has practiced patience.
The Honored Immortal [said]: "Split it apart, yet it remains whole" (also said: "The sword has long since departed").
Upon reaching the home, body and mind are extinguished; movement and stillness are as one. The five desires and the eight winds cannot shake them;

the four modes of birth and the nine realms of existence have no door by which to enclose them. Coming and going within birth and death is profoundly still and empty. Thus it is said: "The essence is tranquil and secure."
When one reaches this state, even if one encounters a sharp blade, one remains composed and fearless; even if one is given poison, one remains at ease.

This is because, as with the Venerable Śāriputra receiving a blade and the Great Master Bodhidharma ingesting poison, they had already realized the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
To cite another example from when our Buddha was on the path of practice: he spread his hair to cover the mud and received a prophecy from Dīpaṃkara Buddha, who said, "In the future..."

In this world, he became a Buddha named Śākyamuni. Furthermore, it is recounted that during many kalpas, while practicing the Way as a Rishi of Forbearance in the mountains, he encountered King Kali, who had entered the mountains with his palace ladies on a hunting expedition.

While the Rishi was sleeping during the day, the palace ladies wandered through the mountains and saw a man sitting alone in solemn stillness; the ladies merely came to gaze upon him, and then the King arose.
He questioned his attendants and palace women as to where they were; his ministers reported, "They have gone to the hermitage of that rishi.
The king, filled with rage, personally took up his sword and asked, "Who are you? They replied, "We are the Rishi of Forbearance.
The king then severed their hands and feet with his sword, dismembering them limb by limb, yet they did not give rise to anger or resentment, even amidst such various forms of suffering.
He remained thus for one kalpa; hence it is said that over many kalpas he was once the Immortal of Forbearance (Kṣāntivādin).
Walking, he was in dhyāna; sitting, he was in dhyāna. This was an immortal who attained the Way while among men.
When someone asked him about the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West, he struck them across the chest with a single forceful fist.
How many times born? (One does not form a single. How many times dead? (Two do not form a pair. Birth and death drift on endlessly, with no fixed end.

(Because there is one, there are two; yet even that one cannot be grasped. Since I have suddenly awakened to the fact that there is no birth, (If it is already non-arising, then how can there be anything to arise?
What sorrow or joy can there be amidst all honors and insults? (Whether one has wisdom or lacks it...)
(Thirty *li*).
True Awakening sighed to himself, saying: "Before I had attained enlightenment, I had already undergone immeasurable births and deaths throughout immeasurable kalpas.
I transmigrated and wandered back and forth without a moment's rest, vainly undergoing saṃsāra within a realm that never shifts, toward a state where there was no dharma of liberation."
Within, one delusively binds oneself, like a spring silkworm spinning its cocoon or an autumn moth rushing toward a lamp. Thus it is said: "Birth and death drift on endlessly, with no fixed end.

Since attaining the sudden realization of the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the forbearance of the non-arising of phenomena), both honor and disgrace have been forgotten, and both sorrow and joy have been extinguished.
What, then, can birth and death possibly have over me?
How many times born? How many times dead? From antiquity to the present, it has always been thus. There are many varieties of divine heads and ghostly faces;
yet in returning to the root and restoring the source, there is not a single atom.

Entering deep mountains (the water becomes turbid when a fish swims); dwelling in an araṇya (feathers fall as birds fly). Amidst towering peaks and secluded depths beneath long pines (a finger is the same as the world;
ten thousand things are the same as a horse), one idly sits at ease in the home of a wild monk (not a single bird carries a flower in its beak).
Dwelling in tranquil seclusion is truly refined and carefree (there is nothing to grasp; it is also said that past and present are clearly distinct).

After receiving the imperial decree, the Ancient One retired into deep mountains and remote valleys. Dwelling in thatched huts and stone chambers, he was accompanied only by his own shadow as he withdrew from the world.
Within the realm of profound stillness, his spiritual awareness shone forth of itself; as the years passed and months deepened, he came to possess great fearlessness.
Following conditions with untrammeled ease and wandering at will as one pleases, the three realms cannot constrain him, nor can the six sense-objects disturb him.
One may truly say he strolls leisurely and sits in tranquility within the home of a wild monk; dwelling in profound stillness, he is truly carefree and elegant.
Entering deep mountains and dwelling in aranyas, one lets go of both the mundane and the supramundane. Pure and naked, there is no ground for assumption;
bare and unadorned, there is nothing to grasp.
Awakening is immediate realization (clouds parting and the moon shines bright). No effort is required (the tiger’s roar stirs the wind).

All conditioned phenomena are not the same (the treasures of Liang have always belonged to Master Zhi). Giving with attachment to signs produces heavenly merit (the Emperor’s decree within the realm).
It is like shooting an upward-pointing arrow into the void (the General’s command beyond the frontier). When its momentum is exhausted (a person’s poverty...)
(Wisdom is short). The arrow falls back (the horse is lean and its hair is long). It brings about an unfavorable future life (when walking at night, do not tread on white;
it is either water or stone). How can this compare to the Gate of Unconditioned True Reality (pointing his finger and saying:
"Enter here")? Transcending in a single leap, one enters directly into the stage of the Tathāgata (one may rejoice, for we have arrived home).
One who has attained awakening is a person of ultimate realization; they have acquired non-effortful wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*), which is distinct from the conditioned practice of meritorious deeds.
Formerly, Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty asked Bodhidharma: "Since I ascended the throne, I have built monasteries, transcribed scriptures, and ordained countless monks."
"What merit is there in this? Bodhidharma replied, "This is a minor fruit of humans and devas, a cause of outflows (*āsrava*);
it is not a great merit. The Emperor asked, "What then is a great merit? Bodhidharma replied, "Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect;

its essence is inherently empty and quiescent. Such merit is not to be sought through worldly means. Emperor Wu was thus stuck on the merits of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*). This is why it is said that one dwells in signs (*nimitta*).
The merit of giving that leads to rebirth in the heavens is like an upward-pointing arrow shot into the void; when its momentum is exhausted, the arrow falls back down.
Thus it is said that one will encounter unfavorable circumstances in future lives. Hanshan said:

"I have seen the Wheel-Turning King, constantly surrounded by a thousand sons, transforming the four continents through the ten wholesome deeds, adorned with many of the seven treasures. These seven treasures were always with him, his adornment..."
How exquisite and wonderful! Yet when the retribution of blessings is exhausted in a single day, one is like a bird perched upon a reed;

one returns to become a worm on a cow’s hump, wandering through the six realms of existence according to the path of karma—how much more so for ordinary worldlings? How can impermanence ever be relied upon? How can it compare to the gate of the unconditioned true mark (*dharmatā*)?

"One transcends directly and enters the stage of the Tathāgata. That which is the unconditioned true mark (*animitta-lakṣaṇa*) is precisely the Dharma-gate of the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa* as the true mark of formlessness.
The "stage of the Tathāgata" refers to the single true Dharma-realm (*eka-dharmadhātu*) in which the prior and subsequent limits are severed.
To grasp this essential meaning is like a prince ascending the throne or a commoner being appointed as a high minister; therefore, it is said that one "directly enters the stage of the Tathāgata."
Awakening is immediate realization; no effort is required. When both self and objects are forgotten, mind and environment are empty. Each branch of the lotus supports the pale moon;
every leaf of the sandalwood fans the fragrant breeze.
If you only obtain the root (the cart does not drive crosswise), you need not worry about the branches (there is no crookedness or interruption in principle).
Like pure lapis lazuli containing a precious moon (the eyes look southeast, but the mind is directed northwest), once you can understand this wish-fulfilling jewel (meeting it, do not pick it up;
as soon as the thought arises, one knows it exists), benefiting self and others will never be exhausted (this is my own home).
(As the person was just speaking of domestic matters).
Since the root is clarified, the branches and leaves naturally flourish. The "root" refers to the nature of inherently existing numinous awareness;
the "branches" refer to the wondrous functions of hundreds of thousands of samādhis and supernormal powers. "Pure lapis lazuli" is a metaphor for being translucent both inside and out.
"Jewel Moon" (Ratnacandra) is a metaphor for the wondrous nature’s perfect luminosity. It is like empty space, which contains all phenomena yet makes no distinctions among any objects;
therefore it is said: "Once one can understand this wish-fulfilling jewel, benefiting oneself and others will never be exhausted.
Without seeking excellence, excellence arrives of its own accord; self-awakening and awakening others constitute an inexhaustible wondrous function."
If you only attain the root, you need not worry about the branches; wondrous function flows freely and boundlessly, as lively as a darting fish.
With a single stroke of the hand, the Gate of Non-duality is flung open; the great chiliocosm is this vast and wide.
The river moon shines (the shrimp leaps from the bottom of the well). The pine wind blows (the magpie cries atop the tree). Throughout the long night and clear evening, what is there to do?
(The thief’s heart is naturally apprehensive. Buddha-nature is the jewel of precepts; it is the seal of the mind-ground (there is no need to hang up an ancient mirror).
Mist, dew, clouds, and mists are the garments upon the body (when dawn breaks, all is naturally clear).
This is the realm of the Great Beings Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra; it is beyond the reach of conceptualization or discrimination. An ancient said:
"To spend thirty years merely regarding this as an objective realm—what could one do during these long, clear nights? It would already be like painting legs on a snake.
To recognize one's own mind is called Buddha-nature; its inner and outer luminous clarity is termed the "precept-jewel," which is capable of giving rise to all dharmas.

It is called the "Mind-Ground" (*cittabhūmi*). It is termed a "Seal" (*mudrā*) because it issues commands to all classes of beings. Although there are many names, their principle is one and the same. Heaven and earth share the same root as I;
the myriad things share the same substance as I. Therefore, it is said: "Mist, dew, clouds, and mists are the garments upon my body."
The river moon shines; the pine wind blows. Where else could one seek Mañjuśrī? Ten ages of past and present are like a flash of lightning;
the ocean of three thousand worlds is but a single thatched hut.

The dragon-subduing bowl (black as lacquer). The tiger-releasing staff (bright as the sun). The two-pronged golden rings chime clearly (unrivaled above, below, and in the four cardinal and intermediate directions).
This is not a mere display of form or a hollow act of holding;
it is the personal trace of the Tathāgata’s precious staff (Dharmatrāta came ten thousand *li* from the West, yet when facing the King of Liang, he said, "I do not recognize you").
The alms bowl is for receiving offerings; the mendicant’s staff is for subduing demons. These two are the personal requisites of the Sangha.
As for what are called the "dragon-subduing bowl" and the "tiger-releasing staff," each acquired its name through a specific historical origin.

In the past, the World-Honored One subdued a fire dragon within his bowl, and eminent monks released two tigers beneath their staffs. As the accounts are numerous, they are not detailed here. [The staff] has two prongs.
The [single] character represents the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional. The six rings represent the six *pāramitās*. The central ring represents the Middle Way.
When the True Awakened One went to Caoxi, he circumambulated the bed three times and struck his *khakkhara* staff once; this indeed has its own source.
It is not that one merely displays external deportment or maintains it as a hollow formality. As the Sūtra says:
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, "You should accept the khakkhara staff. Why is this? Because all Tathāgatas of the past and all Buddhas of the present have held it.
It is the insignia of the sages. Therefore, it is said: "The precious staff of the Tathāgata is the personal trace [of his presence]."
The dragon-subduing bowl; the tiger-unraveling staff. Face-to-face, the opportune moment is personally entrusted. The discourse of three thousand years can no longer be pursued.
One day, I shall have my two instances of being soaked returned.
Not seeking the true (south of the river Xiang), not severing the delusory (north of the lake Tan).

To fully realize that these two dharmas are empty and signless (in the midst lies gold filling the entire land). Signless, empty, and yet not non-empty—this is the Tathāgata’s true mark (under the shadowless tree they share a single boat;
in the lapis lazuli hall there is no one to know).
The two dharmas of reality and delusion are fundamentally provisional names; seeking to sever the two views is likewise a delusion.
For those ordinary beings who seek to sever delusion by pursuing reality and realize a conditioned nirvana, this is not ultimate. The *Lotus Sūtra* says:
"Merely being free from delusion is called liberation, yet in truth one has not attained all-encompassing liberation. If it were the Perfect and Sudden [Teaching]...
Ji understood that these two dharmas are fundamentally empty, signless, and nameless. Fearing that later practitioners might become stuck in emptiness and signlessness, Yongjia further stated:
"Signless, empty, and not non-empty—this is the true mark of the Tathāgata.
This is because the achievements of cultivation and realization vary; thus, the paths of speech and thought are utterly exhausted.
Do not seek truth; do not sever delusion. To attempt to sever seeking is to create a gulf as vast as heaven and earth.
If anyone should further ask how it is so, they shall receive thirty blows across the spine with a single shout.
The mirror of the mind is luminous (the numinous light shines through). Its discernment is unimpeded (transcending the sense organs and their objects).

Vastly clear and penetrating, it pervades the realms of all lands (the essence reveals true permanence, unconstrained by words and letters). Within its reflection, the myriad phenomena are arrayed in dense profusion (the nature of the mind is unstained and fundamentally perfected from the beginning).
This single orb of perfect light is neither internal nor external (simply leave behind delusive conditions, and you are as such).

As with the Buddha, the light of the mind penetrates through and through, fusing with all things without exception. Its tranquil illumination reaches as far as the sands of the Ganges, entirely free from obstruction.

Like a mirror set upon its stand—when a Hu arrives, it reflects the Hu; when a Han arrives, it reflects the Han—the lights interlace and the reflections illuminate one another, mutually penetrating and harmonizing.
They interpenetrate one another; it may be said that the realms of infinite lands are not separated from oneself or others by so much as a hair’s breadth.

The ten ages of past and present, from beginning to end, do not depart from the present moment of thought. The four classes of noble beings and the six realms of ordinary beings—the myriad phenomena of the universe—all flow forth from within my wondrous clarity.
Even such feats as casting this world into another realm or containing Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed are likewise [contained therein].
This is the constant nature of the mind; it does not depend on any external artifice.
When the mirror of the mind is bright, its reflection is unimpeded: within the great, the small appears; within the small, the great appears. All phenomena are thus one and the same.
The Samādhi of Dust upon Dust is cast before one’s face. The lacquer bucket does not understand;
it is a vast, open emptiness (one must not let this pass). One brushes away cause and effect (if you let this pass, it cannot be forgiven).

Vastly and wildly wandering, one invites calamity and disaster (what crime is there in beating someone to death?). Abandoning existence to cling to emptiness—the illness is the same (it strikes the South).
Moving toward the edge [is like moving] toward the north. It is just like avoiding drowning by throwing oneself into fire (look where you step).
Having attained awakening to the correct view, Yongjia took pity on those who study erroneously, being single-mindedly attached to emptiness and denying cause and effect.
Thus he said: "Vast and boundless, without restraint or regulation, they recklessly invite calamity and misfortune. They are like a cowardly man who calls himself an emperor."
The king falsely accuses and executes them. If one abandons the view of existence only to become attached to the view of non-existence, the illness is likewise the same. Thus it is said:
"It is like avoiding drowning only to throw oneself into fire."
To be expansively indifferent to emptiness and to cast aside cause and effect— though these may seem like things brought forth one by one for inspection—
if you further forget your body and lose your resolve, this incurable illness will only grow greater.
To abandon the deluded mind (like searching for a needle at the bottom of the sea) and grasp at ultimate truth (like seeking seams in empty space)—

the very act of grasping and abandoning gives rise to artifice and hypocrisy (to err by a hair’s breadth is to miss by a thousand li). When practitioners do not understand this, they apply themselves to cultivation (like a diseased eye seeing floating flowers in the sky),
thereby deeply committing the error of mistaking a thief for one’s own son (like empty flowers producing empty fruit).

If one wishes to abandon the mind of delusion and grasp the principle of *tathatā* (suchness), yet does not forget the mind of grasping and rejecting, one will consequently fall into conduct that is artful, hypocritical, and insubstantial.
Because students do not understand this point, they merely identify the gateways and thresholds—the clarity and alertness of hearing, seeing, sensing, and knowing—as their own self;
thus, they profoundly commit the error of mistaking a thief for their son.
It is said in ancient times: "Those who study the Way do not recognize the Real, simply because they have long been identifying with the spirit.
This is the root of birth and death throughout immeasurable kalpas; yet fools call it the 'Original Person'."
To abandon the deluded mind and grasp at ultimate truth is like discarding the great ocean while identifying with the substance of a bubble.
One merely observes the bubble arising from the water, yet fails to realize that when the bubble perishes, it returns to the water.
The Dharma-treasure is depleted (the household ghost has entered); merit is extinguished (one is finished being robbed by thieves).

There is nothing that does not stem from this mind-consciousness (a spring breeze fills the ground, leaving it in total disarray). Therefore, in the Chan gate, one brings the mind to an end (when it is thoroughly understood, there is nothing to understand).
One enters suddenly into the power of non-arising knowledge and vision (even at the level of the profoundest mystery, one must still apply censure).
The hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates all converge within the single square inch of the mind; the sands-of-the-Ganges virtues of wondrous merit are all contained within the source of the heart.
This is truly because weary beings lack self-confidence and instead seek outwardly, forcibly establishing themselves as masters over the mind, consciousness, and intellect;

thus, their Dharma-wealth and meritorious virtues are all diminished and extinguished. Hanshanzi said: "Alas, I see the people of this world, forever falling into the ford of delusion throughout kalpas."

If one does not comprehend this meaning, one's cultivation will be nothing but bitter toil. Therefore, the Chan school brings the mind to its ultimate end, entering suddenly into the power of the vision of non-arising.
This is what is meant by the ninefold elixir that transforms iron into gold, or the single word of ultimate truth that transforms the ordinary into the sage.
If you attempt to cross over my school with your mind-consciousness, it is like heading west while intending to go east.
Only by twisting the skin of your face and seeing through directly will you behold the round red sun rising upon the solitary peak.
The Great Man (Lu) wields the sword of wisdom (Xian). The point of Prajñā is like the radiance of a vajra (Jiao).
Not only does it utterly shatter the minds of externalists (Po ye po ye), it has long since caused the hearts of the celestial Māras to fall (Duo ye duo ye).
A great man of the world is one who, with a heart of loyalty and filial piety and a will of fierce resolve,

establishes himself within the halls of state and elevates his sovereign to the heights of Yao and Shun, thereby causing all the common people of the world to rejoice in a peaceful and harmonious governance.
A great man who has transcended the world is a being of great mind who wields the sword of wisdom.
He crushed the demon of the five aggregates and restored that vast expanse beyond the limit of majestic sound—the single, primordial ground of the kalpa before yin and yang arose.
He raised the collapsing thread of the Patriarch who descended from the heavens and was a great master of the North whose lineage filled the sky.
"Prajñā-peak" refers to emptying all existence; "Vajra-flame" refers to annihilating the demonic armies of birth and death.
Therefore it is said: "Not only has he utterly crushed the minds of the externalists; long ago he already caused the courage of the heavenly Māras to fall away.
Do you all see this? After a long silence, he said: "The sword has been gone for a long time, yet you are only now marking the boat on the river. Have you not seen what Master Wuzu Yan said?
Zhaozhou’s drawn sword—its cold frost and blazing radiance. Should you further dare to ask "How is it?", your body shall be split in two.
He shakes the Dharma-thunder and beats the Dharma-drum; spreading clouds of compassion, he sprinkles sweet dew. When dragons and elephants trample through them, all are moistened.

At the boundaries, those of the three vehicles and five natures all awaken. Like the fat of the snowy mountains, pure and without admixture, I constantly receive the purest *amṛta* (clarified butter).
One nature universally penetrates all natures; one dharma universally contains all dharmas.
As the single moon universally appears in all waters, all moon-reflections in the water are subsumed within that one moon. The *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas enters my own nature.
My nature is identical and in union with that of the Tathāgata. In a single stage, all stages are fully perfected. It is neither form nor mind, nor is it karma or its traces.
In the snap of a finger, the eighty thousand gates are perfectly accomplished; in a single instant, three great kalpas are extinguished.
All numerical phrases and non-numerical phrases—what connection do they have with my numinous awakening? (All that has been offered above is entirely in accordance with reality.)
The Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, successive patriarchs, and all spiritual friends throughout the world serve as models for preaching the Dharma and benefiting sentient beings.
First, they awaken them with the thunder of the Dharma; next, they gather them together with the drum of the Dharma;

and finally, they cover them all with the clouds of compassion, moistened by a single rain. Thus, the three types of grasses and two types of trees each attain growth. Therefore, they are called "dragons and elephants."
Treading upon it moistens all boundlessly. Those of the three vehicles and five natures are all awakened. On the Snowy Mountains there is a grass called "Fatty"; it contains no other admixture.
When the white ox eats it, it produces nothing but pure *ghṛta*. The Snowy Mountains are a metaphor for the single true realm;

the fragrant grass is a metaphor for the perfect and upright path; the white ox is a metaphor for wisdom illuminating the ultimate truth; and the *ghṛta* is a metaphor for the supreme flavor of the One Vehicle.
This clarifies that when a Bodhisattva of the Supreme Vehicle first gives rise to the mind of enlightenment, they immediately achieve perfect awakening.

Because those with the capacity for the Perfect and Sudden teaching are in accord with this moment by moment, it is said that they "constantly receive. As Guishan said, "It is not as good as receiving a little bit according to one's lot"—how is this so?
When the single nature is penetrated, then all natures are universally penetrated; when a single dharma is thoroughly realized, then [all dharmas] are pervasive.

It encompasses all phenomena. One then realizes for the first time that sentient beings have been Buddha from the very beginning, dwelling together in the Land of Eternal Quiescent Light, all equally named Vairocana.
It is like the single moon universally appearing in all waters; the moon in every body of water is subsumed within that one moon.
They interpenetrate and merge with one another, layer upon layer, inexhaustibly, and inexhaustibly layer upon layer. This is not merely symbolic.
The Dharma can only be known through direct realization; therefore, it is said that "one stage is fully endowed with all stages.
It is neither form nor mind, nor is it karma or action. "Stage" refers to the stage of self-realization, which is beyond the reach of intellectual understanding.
"Neither form" means it is not obstructive form. "Neither mind" means it is not the mind of sensory cognition. "Neither action" means it is not volitional construction.

This is practice. That which is not karma is that which is not a karma to be performed. It is the state where those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom understand all at once and realize all clearly;
it is what Ānanda referred to as "attaining the Dharma-body without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. This is the ground of arrival.
All natures and characteristics, the hundreds of thousands of Dharma-gates, and the immeasurable subtle meanings are merely provisional expedients and not the ultimate.
The Dharma is ultimately consummate; thus it is said that all numerical phrases and non-numerical phrases have no connection whatsoever with my numinous awakening.
He shakes the thunder of the Dharma and beats the drum of the Dharma; the waters of the sea surge and Mount Sumeru dances. Upon the tip of a single hair, heaven and earth are settled;
throughout the great chiliocosm of dust-motes, there is not a speck of soil.
It cannot be disparaged; it cannot be praised (seated at both ends, cutting them off; a single sword leaning against the sky, cold).
Its substance is like empty space, without shore or limit (the mind does not betray others, and the face shows no shame).

Without leaving its current place, it is eternally profound and still (within the jar is another heaven). If you seek it, you will know that you cannot see it (the sword has long since departed, yet you are only now carving).
A boat. One cannot grasp it (by day one sees the sun); one cannot let go of it (by night one sees the stars).
It cannot be obtained through any intermediary—it is simply obtained as it is (a man does not speak when at peace; water does not flow when level. Also: *qiè*).
The mind of one who has realized the Way is like empty space: vast enough to encompass all without exterior, yet subtle enough to enter all without interior.
It cannot be shaken by worldly words of praise or blame. Without departing from its present location, it is profoundly still and tranquil.
To seek it elsewhere is to have long since missed it. As the ancients said: "Where there is a mind at work, there is surely error; when there is no intention to seek, it is perfectly manifest."
Without support, without desire, without name, and without character; it cannot be grasped, nor can it be relinquished. In a state of carefree spontaneity, one moves with effortless ease.
Within that which cannot be attained, there is simply attainment. This has already been laid open with eight characters and entrusted with both hands.
It is precisely because it is so utterly clear that what is gained seems delayed.
It cannot be disparaged; it cannot be praised. A five-colored qilin strides upon the celestial shore.
If you fail to take this up correctly beneath these words, even the unconditioned will be difficult to escape, as if bound by golden shackles.
Silence when speaking (above is heaven); speech when silent (below is earth). The great gate of giving is open without obstruction (heaven tilts northwest, earth sinks southeast).

When someone asks me what school I understand (the sun is high, the tree shadows deepen), I reply that it is the power of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* (rain falls, the ground becomes damp). Whether this is right or wrong, people—

Consciousness (if recognized, it cannot become an enemy). Its retrograde and forward movements are unfathomable even to the heavens (the thief is a petty person, yet his cunning exceeds that of a gentleman).
I have long practiced through many kalpas (even where there is no elegance, I am elegant).
This is not a casual deception (if you wish to know one string, it consists of two five-hundred coins).
The eloquent speaker has no path of meaning to pursue with others; the silent sage has no state of quiescence to maintain for others.
Master Nantang said: "One who acts as a patriarch must understand that the preaching of the insentient is no different from the preaching of the sentient."
Sentient beings are the devas, humans, and the various classes of living creatures; insentient things are earth, wood, tiles, and stones.

How can you perceive the principle that they are no different? Only by gaining a single eye upon this point will you know that the teaching is proclaimed in every dust mote and in every world-system, burning brightly and without interruption.
Even now, the myriad phenomena of the phenomenal world—both sentient and insentient—are proclaiming it in a vast, surging tide.
Do you hear me? The Sūtra says: "The Buddhas of the ten directions extend their broad and long tongues, completely covering the trichiliocosm, and speak words of truth.
This may be called the opening of the Great Gate of Giving, free from all obstruction.
If someone asks, "What is the fundamental principle that makes it so extraordinary? simply tell them: "It is the power of Mahāprajñāpāramitā! (A sharp rebuke!)
One must avoid making hasty judgments. Whether something is right or wrong, contrary or compliant, even Heaven cannot fathom it, let alone a human being.
Yongjia said of himself: "I have cultivated Prajñā through many kalpas; I am not one who would casually deceive or delude others."
Tangshan said: "If one can never retreat in every successive birth, the stage of Buddhahood may certainly be expected. This is not a false claim.
To speak in silence, and to remain silent while speaking—within the myriad phenomena of the universe, all share a single tongue. There is no distinction between the mundane and the supramundane;
they are spoken of in every dust mote and in every world-system, proclaimed with unceasing fervor.
Raising the Banner of the Dharma (scarifying a healthy wound), establishing the fundamental principle (beating the bone to extract the marrow).
"Clearly and brightly, the Buddha’s decree points to Caoxi"—tell me, what is this? The first, Kāśyapa, was the primary transmitter of the lamp (Xie Sanlang does not recognize the four characters;
the root of the offense has always been you). Twenty-eight generations are recorded in the West (following along).
Furthermore, it is said that they have successively obstructed one another.

To examine the origin of this: the spiritual source is profoundly still and the ocean of Dharma is deep and vast; fundamentally, there is no distinction between names and forms, so how could there be any difference between the holy and the ordinary?
It is simply because sentient beings in their weary existence lack self-confidence, drifting with their karma through kalpas of eons, rising and sinking as they are tossed about.
Thus, they forget themselves and lose their way. Therefore, our Greatly Awakened World-Honored One, exercising compassion that is identical with their own being, acts as an uninvited friend.

For this great causal purpose, he appears in the world and employs various forms of speech and various provisional gateways, causing all sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—just as one exchanges honeyed fruit for bitter gourds. Thus it is said.

It is said: "To erect the Dharma-banner and establish the fundamental tenet. "Dharma" refers to the primordially existing Dharma. "Banner" signifies being lofty and manifest, like a standard or insignia.

"Fundamental tenet" refers to that which is venerated by the multitude; it is the awakening to and clarification of the mind-ground, like stars bowing toward the North Star or waters flowing toward the East.
"Clearly manifest is the Buddha’s command: at Caoxi, the robe shall cease its transmission, while the Dharma shall circulate throughout the sands [of the world]."
Regarding the *dhātu*: Kāśyapa was the first to transmit the lamp of the Dharma.

At the assembly for the *parinirvāṇa*, when the Great Brahmā King offered a golden *pārijāta* flower to the Buddha and offered his own body as a seat to request the Buddha to preach the Dharma, the Buddha took this flower and showed it universally to the great assembly.
While hundreds of thousands of people were all at a loss, only Kāśyapa alone grasped the intent. The world...
The Honored One said: "I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvana, the subtle and wondrous Dharma-gate of formlessness within form.
I entrust this to you as the principle of the 'Separate Transmission outside the Teachings. Therefore, it is said that the lamp was first transmitted.

From this point on, the patriarchs have inherited it one after another, with mind sealing mind. This is recorded in the twenty-eight generations of the Western Heaven: the First Patriarch was Kāśyapa; the Second..."
The First Patriarch was Ānanda; the Third Patriarch, Śaṇakavāsin; the Fourth Patriarch, Upagupta;
the Fifth Patriarch, Diṭṭhika; the Sixth Patriarch, Miśraka; the Seventh Patriarch, Vasumitra; the Eighth Patriarch, Buddhanandi;
the Ninth Patriarch, Buddhamitra; the Tenth Patriarch, Pārśva; the Eleventh Patriarch, Punyayaśas; and the Twelfth Patriarch, Aśvaghoṣa the Great.
The Thirteenth Patriarch was Kāpimāra; the Fourteenth Patriarch was Nāgārjuna; the Fifteenth Patriarch was Kāyatīva; the Sixteenth Patriarch was Rāhulata;
the Seventeenth Patriarch was Saṃghanandi; the Eighteenth Patriarch was Gaya; the Nineteenth Patriarch was Kumāralata;
the Twentieth Patriarch was Śayata; the Twenty-first Patriarch was Vāsukandha.
The twenty-second patriarch was Maṇḍara; the twenty-third, Haklenā; the twenty-fourth, Siṃha;
the twenty-fifth, Vaseṣṭa; the twenty-sixth, Rāhulamitra; the twenty-seventh, Prajñātāra;
and the twenty-eighth, Bodhidharma. Thus it is said that there were twenty-eight generations in the Western Heaven (India).
This refers to the "Recorders.
They erected the banner of the Dharma and established the fundamental tenets; from this point, the root of calamity for the Eastern Land began.
Their poison flowed through the four seas with waves surging to the heavens—how could it have been stopped by encountering but a great wind?
The Dharma flowed eastward (the source of calamity was born). It entered this land (where a fierce tiger blocks the road).

Bodhidharma was the First Patriarch (a jade hare runs upon coral branches). The transmission of the robe through six generations was heard throughout the world (hearing one’s name is not as good as meeting them in person).
As for those who later attained the Way, how could their number be exhausted? (If the sweet melon reaches the stem it is sweet; if the bitter gourd is connected to the root it is bitter.)
In the Sanskrit language, he is called Bodhidharma; here, it is translated as "Awakening to the Dharma. In Western India, he was the twenty-eighth patriarch;
in this land, he is the First Patriarch. He was the third prince of King Xiangzhi of South India and encountered the twenty-seventh patriarch.
Knowing that his secret traces revealed the essential core of the mind, he recorded this, saying: "You must not travel far; remain for now in the Southern Heaven.
Wait sixty-seven years after my extinction, then you shall go to China (Zhendan) and greatly propagate the Buddhist teachings. When you go to the South, do not settle there;
they only delight in conditioned achievements and do not perceive the Buddha-nature. Even if you reach that place, you must not stay long."

He remained there. Listen to my verse: "Traveling along the road, crossing water, one encounters sheep again; Alone and desolate, one silently crosses the river at dusk. At sunset, how pitiable are the pair of elephants and horses;
