Two young cassia trees have long flourished in full splendor. The Master, while in his own country, had refuted the heterodox interpretations of the six schools.
From South India, he sailed across the sea and traveled for three years. This was the ninth month of the eighth year of the Putong era.
On the twenty-first day, they arrived at Guangzhou. The Regional Inspector, Xiao Ang, submitted a memorial to inform Emperor Wu. The Emperor issued an edict for them to come to Jinling.
The Emperor asked, "Since my accession to the throne, I have built temples, transcribed scriptures, and ordained countless monks. What merit do these deeds possess?

The Master replied, "These are merely the small fruits of the human and celestial realms, causes tainted by outflows (*āsrava*). They follow one like a shadow follows a form; though they exist, they are not real. The Emperor—

The Emperor asked, "What constitutes true merit? The Master replied, "Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect; its essence is inherently empty and still. Such merit is not to be sought through worldly means.
The Emperor asked, "What is the primary meaning of the Noble Truths? The Master replied, "Vast and open—there is no 'sage' here. The Emperor asked, "Who is it that stands before me?
The Master replied, "I do not know. The Emperor failed to attain realization. On the nineteenth day of the tenth month...
He returned secretly to the north of the Yangtze River. On the twenty-third day of the eleventh month, he arrived at Luoyang;

this was the tenth year of the Tahe era of Emperor Xiaoming of the Later Wei dynasty. He took up residence at Shaolin on Mount Song, where he sat facing a wall, remaining silent throughout the entire day.
No one could fathom him; he was the First Patriarch of the Chan school. Nine years later, there was a monk named Shenguang.

He was a man of vast and open spirit. Having resided for a long time in the region of the Yi and Luo rivers, he had extensively read the various scriptures and was skilled at discussing the profound principles of the mysteries (*xuanli*). He often sighed, saying:
"The teachings of Confucius and Laozi—regarding ritual arts and social norms—as well as the texts of Zhuangzi and the *Yi*, do not fully exhaust the wondrous principles.

Recently, he heard that the Great Master Bodhidharma was dwelling at Shaolin. Thinking that this sage was not far off and that he would surely reach the profound realm, he went there to attend upon him morning and evening.
[Daokai] replied, "I have received [his instructions]. The Master often sat upright facing a wall, never being heard to offer words of exhortation.

Dazu Hui Guang said to himself, "In the past, those who sought the Way would break their bones to extract marrow, pierce their veins to relieve hunger, spread their hair to cover mud, and throw themselves off cliffs to feed tigers. If the ancients were like this, what person am I?
On the night of the nineteenth day of the twelfth month of that year, it rained and snowed heavily. Hui Guang stood firm and did not move."
The snow accumulated until it reached Da Ming’s knees. The Master took pity on him and asked, "You have stood in the snow for a long time; what do you seek?
Da Ming said with tears of sorrow, "I only pray that the Master, out of compassion, will open the gate of ambrosia to widely deliver all living beings. The Master said:
"The unsurpassed, wondrous path of all Buddhas requires diligent effort through vast eons; one must perform what is difficult to perform and endure what is not easily endured.
How could one hope to attain the True Vehicle with meager virtue and limited wisdom, or with a frivolous and arrogant mind? Your toil and hardship would be in vain.
Having heard the Master’s exhortation, Guang secretly took a sharp blade and severed his own left arm, placing it before the Master. Recognizing him as a vessel for the Dharma, the Master said:

"The Buddhas of all ages first sought the Way for the sake of the Dharma, forgetting their very bodies. You have now severed your arm before me; your seeking is likewise acceptable. He then changed his name to Huìkě.
Huìguāng asked, "May I hear the Dharma-seal of the Buddhas? The Master said, "The Dharma-seal of the Buddhas is not obtained from another.
Huìguāng said, "My mind is not yet at peace; I beg the Master to grant me peace of mind. The Master said, "Bring forth your mind."

"I grant you peace," [the First Patriarch] said. Huikang replied, "I have searched for the mind, but it is ultimately unattainable. The Master said, "I have finished granting you peace. From this, he attained awakening and became the Second Patriarch.
The Second Patriarch received this from the First Patriarch; in all cases, they transmitted the robe and alms bowl as tokens of succession.
Mo transmitted it to Ke; Ke transmitted it to Can; Can transmitted it to Xin; Xin transmitted it to Ren; Ren transmitted it to Neng—this was the Sixth Patriarch, the Great Master of Caoxi.
Upon reaching him, the transmission of the robe ceased, and only the Dharma was transmitted.

From that time onward, those who attained Buddhahood and became patriarchs emerged like surging waters and rising mountains; monasteries and temples were distributed like chess pieces across the stars. Thus it is said: "Those who later attained the Way."
How can its number be exhausted?
The Dharma flowed eastward and entered this land. It opened the gate of heaven and cleared the door of earth; it benefited humans and devas, becoming the patriarch of the Buddhas.
Were one to attempt to conceive of it through thought, in what kalpa could one ever awaken to it?
Truth does not stand (the sun rises in a clear sky). Falsity is fundamentally empty (as the sun climbs high, the flower shadows deepen).

Both existence and non-existence are cast aside, yet it is not a mere emptiness (a single eye at the crown of the head towers above the two pupils). The twenty gates of emptiness have never attached themselves (the void releases a crane soaring to the vast heavens).
The single nature and the Tathāgata’s essence are inherently identical (the customs of Min and Shu are the same).
The wondrous nature is perfectly luminous and free from all names and marks. Originally, there have been no worlds or sentient beings;

it is due to delusion that there is birth, and due to birth that there is cessation. Birth and cessation are called delusion; the cessation of delusion is called truth. Since truth does not stand as something established, its delusion is fundamentally empty.

Both existence and non-existence are discarded; neither is empty, yet it is also empty. Previously, the Tathāgata refuted twenty kinds of views that cling to existence, thereby establishing the names of the twenty emptinesses.
Now, we clarify that the principle of the single nature is not the same as those twenty emptinesses; therefore, it is said that from the beginning there has been no attachment.
When the single nature and the essence of the Tathāgata are inherently identical, one transcends the divergent views of the non-Buddhists and is immediately in accord with the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If the wondrous mind merges in profound stillness, it is said that their essence is inherently identical.
Truth does not stand; delusion is fundamentally empty. With this single phrase fully presented, no blade is revealed: the water flows from West Ravine to East Ravine;
the fire burns on South Mountain while North Mountain glows red.

The mind is the root (a single film over the eye); phenomena are the dust (empty flowers falling in confusion). These two are like scars upon a mirror (only when the mirror is shattered can they meet).
When the stains of the scars are exhausted, the light finally appears (when the one mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are simultaneously stilled).
When both mind and phenomena are forgotten, the nature is the truth (from here to Han-yang is not far).
When humans receive True Suchness (tathatā), that which is not its inherent nature is provisionally called "mind" (*citta*). Receiving phenomena from this mind is called "objects" (*viṣaya*).

Because it takes True Suchness as its condition yet does not maintain its own nature, it can follow along with conditions of either defilement or purity; therefore it is said: "The mind is the root; phenomena are the objects.
These two types are like stains and grime upon an ancient mirror, shrouding the radiance so that it cannot manifest. Thus it is said: "When the stains are exhausted..."

When time and light first appear, mind and phenomena are both forgotten, and one's nature is itself the Truth. An ancient worthy said: "If a single film is in the eye, illusory flowers fill the world;
if a single delusion is in the mind, the sands of the Ganges arise and perish. When the conceptual mind is dissolved, the flowers vanish; when delusion is extinguished, one realizes the Truth.
Therefore, it is said that one's nature is itself the Truth.
The mind is the root; phenomena are the dust. Eight *liang* have always been but half a *jin*.
Laughing, he pulls both ends free at once; upon the eye of a gnat, he strides a qilin.
Alas for the Dharma of the Final Age! In this evil world (eight feet wide and twelve feet long), sentient beings have meager merit and are difficult to discipline (truth cannot mask falsehood).
The Sage is far removed and false views run deep (the ocean may dry up, yet its bottom will be seen; a person dies, yet their heart remains unknown).
Demons are strong and the Dharma is weak, resulting in much resentment and harm (if you see a man’s cheek from behind his head, do not associate with him). Having heard these words...

In the Tathāgata’s gate of sudden teaching (*tun-jiao*), that which is accomplished is accomplished by itself (*cheng-ze zi-cheng*). Regret does not eliminate [karma], like a shattered tile; that which is ruined is ruined by itself (*huai-ze zi-huai*).
When action resides in the mind, there is much joy and little anger; when the calamity resides in the body, there is little joy and much anger.

There is no need for grievance or to blame others (if there is no fiber in one's eyes, one is poor for a lifetime). If you wish not to incur karma of the Avīci Hell, [you must understand] the Dharma... (consciousness)
"Do not slander the Tathāgata’s True Wheel of Dharma" (No clouds arise upon the mountain peaks; the moon descends into the heart of the waves).

This passage expresses Yongjia’s lament that during this degenerate age, the times are evil and the conditions are meager. Since simplicity and sincerity have dispersed, clamor and frivolity flourish daily.
Beings of meager merit do not apply themselves to the Way and its Virtue; they are like mad elephants galloping wild, difficult to subdue.
How much more so for the great sages of the past, who are now long gone?

As their wrong views grew deeper, they instead gave rise to resentment and malice toward the True Dharma—just as when Dharmatrāta’s tooth fell out and the Second Patriarch was harmed by poison. If even such holy masters met with such fates, what need is there to mention those who came after?
Furthermore, some scholars confine themselves to their own interpretations and follow their respective lineages; thus, they brandish the weapons of debate against one another in mutual attack.

Striking [at others], they take what little they have gained as sufficient and do not recognize their own faults. Upon hearing the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Perfect and Sudden Dharma-gate, they instead regard it as erroneous.
They harbor resentment that it has not been extinguished, shattered like crumbling walls or melting ice.

Thus, because of this deluded mind, the immeasurable and boundless black karma they create follows them like a shadow follows a form; hence it is said, "The calamity rests upon the person," and the retribution experienced is immeasurable and boundless.
All bitter fruits are self-inflicted and self-received; they do not result from the actions of others. Thus it is said: "There is no need for grievance or to blame others.
The sin of slandering the Dharma is clearly explained in detail throughout the sutras. If you wish to avoid the grave karma of the Avīci Hell, cease slandering the Tathāgata’s True Wheel of Dharma.
As for the True Dharma, it is that which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have realized and thereby attained unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
The Samyaksaṃbuddhas [have taught this]. Beings of the six realms, diverse in kind, are deluded by this and revolve through the three miserable paths.
Though devas and nāgas protect it, the sin of one who slanders it and does not believe is evident to know.
Alas for the final Dharma! Alas for this degenerate age! Lacking faith in the Tathāgata’s primary truth, one’s body and mind are busily occupied, unaware of one's errors;
in the vast expanse of the ocean of suffering, one sinks and falls by oneself.
In a sandalwood grove (if you mention one, you cannot mention two), there are no other trees (letting one pass, you fall into the second).
Dense and profound, where lions dwell (holding a night-bright talisman in hand, how many know when dawn breaks?).
The realm is tranquil and the forest secluded; he wanders alone (the traveler is further beyond the green mountains). Beasts and birds alike keep their distance.

"Traveling ten thousand *li* while gazing toward one's hometown" refers to the analogy of the sandalwood forest as the single true Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). "Only this one reality exists, with no other trees" means that the other two vehicles are not the truth;
for this is the realm of the Bodhisattvas of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), which cannot be intermingled with the limited capacities of the two vehicles. It is dense and profound.

"The forest-dwelling lion abides. This refers to what is said in the *Lotus Sūtra*: "Profound, firm, remote, and far-reaching; no one can reach it. Once reached, the mountains are green and the waters are lush;
it is not of this human world. It accords only with those of superior capacity; for those of middling or inferior faculties, entry through awakening is difficult at first.
"In the quiet realm and amidst the forest, he wanders alone"—for the lion roams without seeking companions. He casually bellows once—

The sound alone was sufficient to split the skulls of the hundred beasts; thus it is said that "the running beasts and flying birds all fled far away"—this refers to those who withdrew from their seats during the *Lotus Sūtra*.
In a sandalwood forest, there are no other trees; when the Great Function manifests, it is simply this. When Niaoke picked up his cloth...
The whiskers bristle. One who understands and penetrates will awaken at that very moment.

A lion cub (has emerged from its den). The crowd follows behind (chasing shadows and tracking footprints). At three years old, it can already let out a great roar (it is not permitted to travel by night;
one must arrive with the break of dawn). If it were a jackal pursuing the Dharma King (the words have already been inscribed...).
[The character] "three" (三) is a scribal error. A hundred-year-old monster opens its mouth in vain (like the saying "how could *wu* become *yan*, or *an* become *ma*").

What is called the "lion cub" is a metaphor for a Bodhisattva who, upon first generating the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), immediately attains perfect awakening and transcends the various followers of the Lesser Vehicle, such as the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;
hence it is said that "the multitude follows behind. The "three years" symbolize those who have realized their own nature (*jìngxìng*).

The three dharmas are cultivated in a perfect manner: namely, emptiness (śūnyatā), the provisional (upāya), and the middle (madhyama). Emptiness eliminates all phenomena; the provisional establishes all phenomena;

and the middle unifies all phenomena. Emptiness is not fixed as emptiness; within the locus of emptiness, its very essence is both the middle and the provisional. The provisional is not fixed as the provisional;
within the locus of the provisional, its very essence is both emptiness and the middle. The middle is not fixed as the middle; within the locus of the middle, its very essence is...
Emptiness is itself the provisional. These three dharmas are neither vertical nor horizontal, neither simultaneous nor distinct.

In one place there are always three; in three places there is always one. Thus it is said: "The three truths and the three contemplations—three yet not three. Three, one, and one, three; they have no fixed locus."

Contemplating with clarity, one sees that while names differ, their substance is the same; thus, the subject and object are neither two nor not-two. The practitioner who attains realization cultivates these three dharmas in their perfection.
All the dharma-gates taught are the true meaning of the Middle Way; hence it is said: "At three years of age, one can already let out a great roar."
Those of the two vehicles and ordinary beings at various provisional stages cannot clearly perceive the Buddha-nature;

what they say is not real, and even if they open their mouths, it ultimately provides no benefit. Thus it is said: "If a jackal pursues the Dharma King, this monster will vainly open its mouth for a hundred years."
The lion cub is followed by the crowd; a single phrase meets the occasion, cutting off all traces.
Sometimes he picks it up and shows it to people, but by the time they blink their eyes, they have already missed it.
The Perfect and Sudden Teaching (When meeting, do not bring it forth; as soon as the intention arises, one knows it exists).

Do not follow human sentiment (The eyes are born triangular; the head is sharp like the Five Peaks). If there is doubt that cannot be resolved, you must strive for it (Ants returning are hard to find their holes;
birds returning easily see their nests). This is not the mountain monk’s way of asserting self and other (I call it fire; you must not call it fire).
Fire). In practice, one fears falling into the pit of annihilationism or eternalism (clouds stretching across the sea).
"Neither not" (the past is the present); "not not" (the present is the past). To err by a hair’s breadth is to lose a thousand li (a fierce tiger enters a bustling market).
If it is "is," then the Dragon Girl suddenly attains Buddhahood (cloudless sky gives birth to peaks above); if it is "not," then Śunakṣatra falls into the abyss.
[The moon] falls into the waves (the character for "fall" contains the radical for "moon").
The Perfect and Sudden [teaching] is not gradual. The teaching is the vessel that carries the Way. Do not treat this as a matter of ordinary human sentiment;
because the matter of birth and death is of great importance, it cannot be compared to worldly common sense. One must thoroughly awaken to the heart-essence of all Buddhas.
To thoroughly penetrate the core of a monk’s realization, where two eyes face one another and needle and magnet meet, only then will there be a partial correspondence.
If even the slightest doubt remains unexhausted, you must resolve it by asking directly.

Long ago, when the Layman Wujin first studied under Chan Master Zhaojue Zong of Donglin, he attained the principle of "plain reality" and considered himself fully accomplished and completely certain. However, upon meeting Doushui Yue...
The questioner asked, "Sir, you do not deceive yourself in your heart. Regarding the one thousand seven hundred cases of karmic conditions in our school, do you still have any doubts?
Wujin said, "I have no doubts regarding the others; it is only the case of Deshan’s bowl that remains. Yue said, "I have doubts about this very point.
How could I possibly have no doubts about the rest? It is simply this: as for Deshan’s final word, does it exist or not?"
Wujin said, "He says there is," and Yue laughed heartily and returned to his quarters. That night, Wujin was gripped by doubt;
at the fifth watch, he rose and kicked over his footstool, whereupon he suddenly attained great enlightenment. At dawn, he presented this verse: "The drum falls silent, the bell has ceased;
returning with the alms bowl, Yantou’s single thrust was like a clap of thunder. Indeed, I shall live for only three more years— Could it be that I have received his transmission?"
He recorded his arrival, and only then did Yue grant his permission. From this point on, he was like a long sword leaning against the heavens—dare anyone dare meet his blade?

Yongjia said of himself, "This is not a mountain monk indulging in a mind that races after self and others. I fear deeply that later generations might misapply their body and mind, falling into the two views of annihilationism and eternalism.
Because these can trap people, they are called 'pits. It is neither 'not' nor 'is,' neither 'is not' nor 'is it not'; this is what constitutes clarity."
The distinction between right and wrong is clear and cannot be confused. Is it not that what is "non" (wrong) is truly non?
Is it not that what is "is" (right) is truly is? One must not obscure the Buddha-nature or treat True Suchness as a mere abstraction.
Therefore, it is said: "To err by a hair's breadth is to lose a thousand li. Thus, while the Dragon Girl attained Buddhahood instantaneously, Sūryagarbha was reborn in hell.
This illustrates the gravity of the distinction between right and wrong. Formerly, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, there was a dragon girl who offered a precious jewel to the Buddha.

The World-Honored One accepted it and preached the Dharma for her; she immediately realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and departed for the stainless world in the south, where she sat upon a precious lotus flower and attained perfect enlightenment, becoming known as the Tathāgata Padmottara. Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu...

His name was Śunakṣatra (Shanxing). Although he could recite eighteen *dhāraṇīs* concerning fragrant elephants, he did not understand the Buddha’s intent and fell into hell while still in his physical body.
This is because, failing to comprehend the Buddha-nature, he instead fell into slander. Thus, he is cited here to serve as a warning for future generations.
The Perfect and Sudden Teaching—do not let it become a mere matter of human sentiment. Turning one’s body around, one tramples down the city of Nirvana;
from beyond the age of Wei-yin until this very day, a single stretch of radiant splendor cannot be captured in a painting.

Since my early years, I have accumulated learning (the poor man thinks of old debts). I have also sought out commentaries and explored the sūtras and śāstras (those who do not undergo bitter toil do not know this).
Distinguishing names and characteristics, I knew no rest (do not speak of sorrow to one already in sorrow).
Entering the sea to count the sands, I only exhausted myself (speaking to one in sorrow only increases their sorrow). Yet I was instead...
Come to be bitterly rebuked (admitting one's faults as they are). What benefit is there in calculating the treasures of others? (It is difficult to reverse a confession made at the point of death.
From long ago you have stumbled, realizing your journey was in vain (the ground beneath your feet is solid).
For many years you have needlessly been a traveler in the dust (if you wish to know the path down the mountain, simply ask those who come and go).
This is Yongjia’s own account of his youth, when he frequented various lecture halls to study and practice the Tiantai teachings and contemplations.

He thoroughly mastered the sutras and treatises and became refined and rigorous in the Vinaya. Only after this did he seek out spiritual friends to resolve the questions of birth and death. Were it not for the existence of the seeds of the Mahāyāna from past lives, how could one be capable of such things?
He further remarked: "To differentiate the names and characteristics of the five teachings without knowing when to rest is like entering the ocean."
Counting sands only exhausts oneself in vain. This brings to mind the Buddha’s rebuke of Ānanda:

"Though you have, throughout kalpas, cultivated and maintained the secret and wondrous adornments of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, it is not equal to practicing untainted karma for a single day. It is like a person counting another's treasures;
he himself has no share of even half a coin. From the beginning, I have been a failure, realizing I have been a practitioner in name only, racing through births since immeasurable kalpas past.
This is the perilous path of death. You have merely traveled in vain upon the road to Nirvana without ever treading it firmly. It is like a drifting gourd acting as a traveler;
the homeland grows ever more distant. Thus it is said: "In vain you act as a guest of the wind and dust."
Seeking the last traces of red among the treetops and beneath them: one petal flies west, another east. It is but that the peach blossoms were greedy to form fruit;
they have wrongly caused people to resent the wind of the fifth watch.
Those of the wrong lineage (like those with diseased eyes seeing flowers in the sky) have mistaken understanding (like flowers in the sky producing fruits from the void).
They fail to reach the Tathāgata’s perfect and sudden teaching (one constantly remembers that in the third month in Jiangnan, where the partridges cry, the hundred flowers are fragrant).

Those of the Two Vehicles exert diligence but lack the Bodhicitta (when a person is poor, their wisdom is short). Those of the external paths possess cleverness but no true wisdom (the horse is lean).
The hair grows long; they are likewise deluded. They are also slightly startled (the same pit has no different soil).

From an empty fist pointing upward, they give rise to a realization of reality (they are fond of digging one pit in empty space to bury it). Taking the finger for the moon, they labor in vain (chasing shadows and pursuing the wind).
Among the dharmas of the sense bases and their objects, one falsely fabricates the extraordinary (buying and selling for oneself).
When not seeing a single dharma, that is the Tathāgata (the oyster holding the bright moon; the jade hare conceiving the fetus). Only then can one be named Avalokiteśvara (a match made in heaven).
Once realized, karmic obstacles are originally empty (realized). If not yet realized, one must still repay past debts (defeated). Like encountering a king’s banquet when hungry.

They cannot eat. When a sick person encounters a King of Physicians, how could they fail to recover? (The lion bites the man; the hound chases the clod. Their spiritual lineage is perverse and not the true cause.
Such practitioners of the Way are actually seeds of external paths (*tīrthika*). By relying on perverse teachers, they give rise to various false views;
hence it is said that their understanding is mistaken. They are unable to penetrate the Tathāgata’s perfect and sudden Dharma-gate.
Throughout immeasurable kalpas, one undergoes immeasurable births and deaths; all of this is due to following false teachers.

Those of the Two Vehicles sever the defilements of the twenty-five states of existence within the Triple Realm and transcend birth-and-death with its segmented limits, much like a gazelle leaping alone without looking back at the herd.
Therefore, it is said: "Do not speak of the Bodhicitta. The non-Buddhists of the Western Heavens possess extreme cleverness, yet they do not understand the Buddha.
To seek the Dharma outside of one's own nature-mind is called being a non-Buddhist (tīrthika). Therefore, it is said that they are both ignorant and foolish.

The lack of wisdom in an adult is called ignorance; the lack of wisdom in a child is called folly. To produce understanding based on words and thereby give rise to attachment is like producing a notion of reality from an empty fist or a pointing finger.
The teachings of the Sūtras are like the finger pointing at the moon; if one turns back to see the moon, one will clearly understand.

That which is pointed out is ultimately not the moon. Those who study the Path do not understand Buddha-nature; they falsely give rise to conceptual understanding based upon the sense organs, objects, and consciousness.
Therefore it is said: "To grasp the finger as the moon is to labor in vain. Within the phenomena of the sense organs and objects, they falsely fabricate strange delusions.

Not seeing that even a single dharma is the Tathāgata—since all dharmas from the very beginning have always been in a state of quiescent extinction—then both existence and non-existence are [equally unreal].
By dispatching the six sense-faculties so that they function interchangeably, one is then called Avalokiteśvara. "Arriving" refers to the field [of realization]:

thoroughly penetrating that the nature of offenses is fundamentally empty and free from all obstructions. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "When one person awakens to the truth and returns to the source, the voids of the ten directions are entirely dissolved;
how much more so the marks of offense and merit? A monk asked an ancient worthy: "If one realizes it, then karma..."
The hindrances are originally empty. As for whether Venerable Siṃha and the Second Patriarch Master were enlightened or not, it is said:
"Do you not see that they are originally empty? Master Sengzhao said: "The five aggregates are fundamentally non-existent; the four elements are originally empty.
To bring one's head to the white blade is just like cutting through the spring breeze. Therefore, it is called "originally empty. If one does not understand this...

Awakening. To cling to dharmas without forgetting them is for cause and effect to remain as distinct as a shadow follows a form. Thus it is said: "If you have not yet realized it, you must repay your past debts.
Since the successive emergence of the sages of old, they have opened the gate of skillful means to reveal the true reality.
This is truly because sentient beings lack self-confidence and are unable to awaken and enter [the truth]. It is like a person in the world suffering from hunger who happens upon...
Regarding the various delicacies in the meals of a king, one immediately feels fear and does not dare to eat them. It is also like a long-term illness that fails to heal;
upon meeting a King of Physicians, one instead gives rise to doubt and refuses to take the wondrous medicine, willingly enduring the suffering of the disease. Thus it is said:
"How can one hope for recovery?"

If one's spiritual lineage is mistaken and their understanding is erroneous, they will run outward in pursuit and remain in self-obscuration. By turning the light inward and reflecting back upon oneself, one returns home;
the numinous root becomes vast and penetrating, free from directionality or bias.

Practicing dhyāna amidst desire through the power of knowledge and vision (39.27), a lotus born within fire can never be destroyed (in his own house, there is naturally one who loves those with spiritual penetration).
Vīradatta committed a grave offense yet awakened to non-arising;
he attained Buddhahood long ago and remains even now (by the stream, the shadows of willows do not obstruct the passage of the fishing boat).

If one has been perfumed by the seeds of the Vehicle in past lives and wears the wheel of great vows upon oneself, even while dwelling amidst the five desires and the eight winds, one will not be turned by those five desires and eight winds.
Standing tall and solitary like a lotus flower in the midst of fire, one is ultimately indestructible.
This is exemplified by such masters as Minister Pei, Yang Wuweishi, Dongpo, Huang Shan谷, Wujin, and Zishao. A monk asked:
"An ancient worthy said: 'In the desire realm there is no dhyāna. Great Virtue, why do you say that there is meditative concentration? The Worthy One replied:
'The Acharya only knows that there is no dhyāna in the desire realm; he does not know that within the realm of dhyāna there is no desire.

When one reaches this stage, even managing one's livelihood and engaging in worldly occupations are entirely non-contradictory with the true mark (dharmatā). Therefore, it is called the power of knowledge and vision. Long ago, in the distant past, there was a bhikṣu.
Named Yongshi (Vīradatta), he suddenly committed a transgression against the Tathāgata’s prohibitions and precepts. Having incurred one of the four grave root offenses, he sought to purify himself;
he hung his three robes upon his mendicant’s staff and cried out in a loud voice, "I have committed a heavy offense;
who will perform my confession? While crying out in this manner, he arrived at a monastery where he encountered an elder named Bi (Ghrāṇa).
Kutala said, "When one investigates the nature of transgression, it is ultimately ungraspable. The bhikṣu Yoṅshi (Vīradatta) attained sudden and great enlightenment;
he immediately proceeded to a world in the southern direction where he realized equal and perfect awakening, receiving the name Tathāgata Ratnacandra.
He remains there even to this day. Therefore it is said: "Yoṅshi committed a grave offense, yet awakened to non-arising; having early attained Buddhahood, he abides even now."
Exercising meditative concentration within the realm of desire through the power of knowledge and vision—midday under a clear blue sky, a thunderclap resounds!
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the most profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Lion’s Roar (the clay ox runs across the snowy peaks); the fearless discourse (empty space bites the tongue).

Deeply lamenting the dull-witted and stubborn hide (how can the deaf hope to hear?), they know only that committing grave offenses obstructs Bodhi (greedily gazing at the moon in the sky), yet fail to see the Tathāgata’s revelation of the secret key (losing the oar from one's own hand). There were two bhikṣus who committed [offenses].
Adultery and murder (a black ox lies dead in the water); Upāli’s fireflies increase the bonds of sin (a leprous horse tied to a withered stake).
The Great Being Vimalakīrti suddenly dispels all doubts, just as the blazing sun melts frost and snow (an eighty-year-old enters the examination hall;
this is truly no child’s play).
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas expound the Mahāyāna with mastery and fearlessness, just as a lion roars without any dread.

"Deeply sighing" (*shēn jiē*) and "extremely lamenting" (*jí tàn*) are words expressing profound sorrow. "Dull-witted" (*mò dǒng*) means lacking intelligence. "Wan pí zhà" refers to the coarse and thick hide on the neck of an ox;
this metaphor illustrates how those of dull faculties in the Hīnayāna do not awaken when hearing the Mahāyāna, thereby giving rise to such lamentation. Only.

To know the karmic obstacles of having committed the four preceding grave offenses (*ānantarya*) means that one cannot yet realize that the nature of sin is empty within the Tathāgata’s treasury of the true Dharma-eye.
There were two bhikṣus who committed sexual misconduct and killing; although Upāli [warned them], their karmic fetters increased like the light of a firefly.
Long ago, there were two bhikṣus who built huts in the mountains to practice, strictly maintaining the pure precepts without any transgression. One day, one of the bhikṣus...
The Buddha went out. A certain bhikṣu was practicing dhyāna-concentration in a hut when he suddenly fell asleep.
A wood-gathering girl violated his pure precepts; consequently, the bhikṣu felt displeasure in his heart. When the fellow monk returned to the hut, he related the matter in full.
That monk became enraged and drove the girl away. Startled and terrified, she fell into a pit and died. The bhikṣu’s afflictions increased further, and they went together to the Venerable Upāli.
They left the Venerable’s presence to seek repentance, but the Venerable judged their offense according to the Hīnayāna.

At that time, the two bhikṣus were plagued by doubt and indecision, which gave rise to further affliction and confusion. The Great Being Vimalakīrti rebuked Upāli for his improper observation of their capacities.
These two bhikṣus had long cultivated the Mahāyāna; how could one take the great ocean and pour it into the hoofprint of an ox? Therefore, it is said: "like the light of a firefly."
This increases the fetters of sin. The Great Being said: "The nature of sin is thoroughly investigated and found to be unobtainable; it is not within, not without, and not in between.
It does not go to the prior limit, it does not come from the posterior limit, and it does not abide in the middle limit. When sought throughout the three limits, it is utterly unobtainable.
At that moment, the two bhikṣus suddenly attained sudden enlightenment and realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), just as the brilliant sun dissolves [the darkness].
Frost and snow;
the lion’s roar, spoken without fear. Ten thousand apertures of raging wind overturn with a single tongue;
the tabby cat and the white ox both hide their tracks, while the pillar and the lantern give rise to joy.
Inconceivable! The power of liberation (a single drop of ink and a stroke of water produce dragons in two places).
Its wondrous function is as infinite as the sands of the Ganges (an inch is not equal to a foot). To offer the four requisites, how could one dare decline the toil?
(What need is there for *bìluó* [dumplings]? Eat them quickly and bring them down! Even ten thousand taels of gold can be consumed by it (A single hand does not clap; both hands must ring together).
Powdering my bones and shattering my body would not suffice to repay [this debt] (where there was no reason, there is now reason).
A single phrase, clearly realized, transcends ten billion worlds (the pure breeze pervading the earth—how could it have limits?).
That which is inconceivable cannot be grasped by the mind or deliberated upon by the mouth. Thus, a sutra says:

"Even if the entire world were filled with those like Śāriputra, and they were to exhaust their thoughts to measure it together, they could not fathom the Buddha's wisdom. This is because the Buddha’s wisdom is unfathomable.
One must instead achieve a profound awakening to one’s own mind, such that one shares the same vision and hearing, and the same realization, as all the sages of antiquity.
Functioning thus, the mundane and supramundane are forged into a single whole; even laughter, scolding, anger, and abuse are all Buddha-activities.
Therefore it is said that "wondrous functions are as vast as the sands of the Ganges and infinite. Upon reaching this stage, one is worthy of receiving offerings from humans and devas;
hence it is said that "ten thousand taels of gold can be consumed. The four requisites are: first, clothing; second, bedding; third, food and drink; and fourth, medicine.
An ancient worthy said: "If an elder has truly attained awakening, he could transform the great earth into gold and churn the long river into cream and curd;

to offer these to the elder would not be considered excessive. Yet, if this is not yet the case, then every grain of rice and every strand of silk must be earned by him through the toil of plowing and harrowing before it can be returned to him.
'To crush one's bones and shatter one's body would not suffice as recompense'—this is like the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita."
Śākyamuni Buddha, in his causal stage, beat his bones to extract the marrow to purchase flowers for an offering to the Buddha, seeking the Dharma;
by this he instantly transcended twelve kalpas behind Maitreya.

Even among our predecessors, the elders, their ground was opened and their hearts penetrated by a single word, and within a single scroll the sky of meaning shone brightly. Thus it is said: "A single phrase, clearly realized, transcends [all]."
Ten billion [worlds]. As clearly explained in detail in the sutras, the text is too voluminous to recount here.
Inconceivable is the power of liberation; spanning from antiquity to the present, it is as bright as the sun.
When Bodhidharma came ten thousand *li* from the West, he faced the King of Liang and said, "I do not know the Way. (Aha! One must strictly avoid boring through tortoise shells or striking tiles.

The King of Dharmas (the heavens upon his crown), the Most Supreme (his feet treading the earth), realized by all Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—(a thousand hearings are not equal to one seeing;
it is also said: "this is like raising waves where there is no wind").
I now understand this wish-fulfilling jewel; those who receive it with faith will all be in accord—(empty space cannot contain it, the great earth cannot support it).
Among kings, the Dharma King’s rank surpasses that of a hundred kings; he transcends the three realms and strides alone upon the Great Vehicle.
Therefore, it is said to be "supremely victorious. All Buddhas of the past, present, and future, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have realized this Dharma.
Initial awakening merges with original awakening; because one awakens oneself and awakens others, it is said that "we together realize it.

I have now understood and awakened to this Dharma, which is like a wish-fulfilling jewel that produces inexhaustibly. The Fourth Patriarch said to Chan Master Niu-tou Rong: "A hundred thousand dharma-gates all return to the single square inch of the mind;
the merits of the Ganges sands are all contained within the source of the heart. All gates of precepts and gates of meditative concentration..."
The gates of wisdom and the gates of practice are all fully perfected. The wondrous functions of the supernormal powers reside entirely within your own mind.

Afflictions and karmic obstructions are fundamentally empty and quiescent. There is no triple world from which to escape, and there is no Bodhi to be sought. Sentient beings and non-sentient beings are equal in their essential nature.
The Great Way is vast and open, transcending thought and beyond deliberation. Such a Dharma as this you have now attained; there is nothing further—
It is without deficiency and no different from that of the Buddha. Simply believe in the sovereignty of your own mind; do not perform contemplative practices, nor do you need to still the mind.

Be vast and unimpeded, moving freely as you wish. Neither performing good deeds nor committing evil acts, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—whatever meets the eye or encounters the conditions—is all the wondrous function of the Buddha. Therefore it is said: "Those who believe and accept it will all be in accord."
The King of Dharmas, most supreme and victorious, horizontally grasps the Mo-ye sword to issue the correct command; across the realm of Great Peace, he beheads the ignorant and the obstinate.
Even if a Buddha were to appear, he would beg for his life.
Clearly seeing: not a single thing (Sun-Face Buddha, Moon-Face Buddha);

neither person nor Buddha (rising in the east and sinking in the west, rising in the south and sinking in the north). The great trichiliocosm is a bubble on the ocean (a single arrow felling two eagles).
All noble sages are like a flash of lightning (already missed).

Even if an iron wheel were to spin upon one’s head (a monkey climbing a tree with its tail reaching the sky), their perfect clarity of concentration and wisdom would never be lost (the hands hang down past the knees).
Within the realm of True Suchness (*tathatā*), the provisional designations of "sentient beings" and "Buddhas" are utterly extinguished. In the state of equality, there are no forms of self or other;
thus, there is no person, no thing, and no Buddha. The trichiliocosm of sand-grain worlds exists within the nature of awakening, arising and ceasing in disorder like bubbles floating upon water.
Therefore it is said: "Emptiness arises within Great Awakening, like a single bubble emerging from the ocean."

When the bubble has vanished, emptiness is fundamentally non-existent; how much more so, then, are the various realms of the three worlds? All the sages and worthies arise one after another, yet they pass away in the blink of an eye.
Like sparks from a flint or a flash of lightning, they are ultimately difficult to grasp. Therefore it is said: "All sages and worthies are like a flash of lightning."
As for the "iron wheel spinning upon the crown of the head": once, a Mara King said to various Bodhisattvas, "You must relinquish your positions.
If you do not relinquish them, I shall fly a glowing iron wheel and spin it above your heads, shattering your bodies into fine dust.
At that time, because the Bodhisattvas possessed the inconceivable power of the perfect clarity of meditative concentration and wisdom, they did not lose their positions.
At that time, the hosts of Māras will instead retreat and lose their advantage. This passage from *The Perpetual Peace* (Yǒngjiā) uses an analogy for the practitioner of the Way:
even if adverse or favorable conditions should arise before them, if they remain as if neither hearing nor seeing them, they will not be deluded by the "skandha-māra" of birth and death.
Seeing clearly, there is not a single thing. Right before one's eyes, a falcon from the vast heavens is unleashed;
the ocean of three thousand worlds is utterly unobstructed, and the ten-thousand-mile void is pierced by a single thrust.
The sun may grow cold; the moon may grow hot (no sinews beneath the eyes, blood beneath the skin).
No demons can destroy the True Teaching (not two tongues in one mouth). The majestic elephant-vehicle advances in vain upon the road (the army follows the seal’s turn;
the general pursues the talisman’s path). Who has seen a mantis able to block the tracks? (Brandishing a staff to strike at the moon. A great elephant does not roam [in such places].
Following the rabbit’s path (heeding the command), a great awakening is not constrained by minor details (Linji and Deshan obtained but a single wedge).
Do not slander the vast heavens with your narrow views (Xie Sanlang on the fishing boat).
For those who have not yet realized it, I shall now resolve it for you (ten thousand miles away, a single piece of iron).
The nature of the sun is inherently hot; how could it be said to be cold? The nature of the moon is inherently cold; how could it be said to be hot?

Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, this alone is the one true reality; any other two are not real. Although the hosts of Māras may attempt to do so, they cannot destroy my teaching of this One Truth.
As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "The Buddha taught that the Four Noble Truths cannot be made otherwise. Thus Yongjia quotes it.
This serves as proof: namely, that the Mahāyāna Dharma-gates propagated by Bodhisattvas cannot be obstructed by any demons.
It is like a majestic elephant carriage advancing in full array; how could a tiny insect such as a mantis ever block its path?
Formerly, when Duke Zhuang of Qi was out hunting, there was a mantis that raised its legs as if to strike his chariot wheel.
He asked his charioteer, "What kind of insect is this? The charioteer replied, "This is a mantis. Duke Zhuang said, "With such minute strength..."
Yet they refuse the great carriage and fail to measure their own strength. Now, Yongjia briefly cites this as evidence to make it easy for people to understand;
thus he says: "Who has seen a mantis able to block a chariot track?

That a great elephant does not travel on a rabbit's path symbolizes the perfect and sudden realm of the Mahāyāna—how could it involve the narrow trails of the human-heaven realms or the Hīnayāna? Great awakening is not constrained by the small.

As for "matters of minor propriety": for one who has realized their nature, it is sufficient that they value the fundamental, possess correct understanding, and have the eye of wisdom perfectly clear and bright.
Being indifferent to worldly affairs and speaking without refined elegance are merely matters of minor propriety. I often see people of our time, my brothers, say:
"One must not be constrained by the observance or violation of the precepts. This is a mistaken statement. The Buddhas of the three periods and the patriarchs of successive generations...

As for the "Good Knowledge of the World" (Śāstra on the Good Knowledge of the World), who among them could have used their own practice to deliver others? Therefore, I have recorded this to correct their errors.
The Perfect and Sudden Great Teaching only connects with those of superior faculties.

If those of small roots, small capacities, shallow understanding, and inferior wisdom wish to peer into the realm of the Mahāyāna, it is like grasping a tube to look at the sky and saying the sky is small; this is not the fault of the sky. Thus it is said:
I have not yet clarified this; let me now resolve it for you. The final phrase is where one first reaches the secure barrier.
When the Great Function manifests, there is no fixed standard. To reveal what existed prior to the empty kalpa is not separate from the present moment.

Have you not seen it said: "What is the 'True Person of No Station'? It is a dried-up piece of dung. This single phrase possesses both illumination and function, and it possesses both provisional and ultimate aspects.
There is the real, there is the guest, and there is the host. If a person can examine and discern this, I grant that they have personally realized the Dharma-gate of the letter A.
If it is otherwise, you shall receive thirty painful blows of the staff and depart of your own accord.
The sun may become cold; the moon may become hot. Yet all Buddhas equally extend their broad and long tongues, for in the world there is only this one Truth.
In the heavens, there is no second moon.
The Song of Realizing the Way by the Great Master Zhizhe of Yongjia:
The Way of the direct pointing transmitted solely from the Western Patriarch originally allows not even a hair’s breadth to be grasped or examined by others;
it exists only in one’s own self-realization and self-awakening, reaching the ground where there is neither realization nor awakening. Therefore, the Great Master Zhizhe traveled extensively...

He was instructed to enter through awakening to conditions (*pratyaya*). He proceeded directly to Caoxi for formal recognition (*abhyanujñā*). Upon his arrival, he encountered the Patriarch during his period of seated meditation.

The Master circumambulated the seat three times, struck his mendicant’s staff once, and stood there with solemn composure. The Patriarch said, "A śramaṇa possesses three thousand dignified deportments (*īryāpatha*) and eighty thousand subtle practices;
in every action, nothing should be deficient. From what direction have you come, Venerable One, that you give rise to such great self-importance?"
The Master said, "The matter of birth and death is great; impermanence is swift. The Patriarch said, "Why do you not realize non-arising and comprehend that there is no swiftness?
The Master said, "Realizing it, there is no arising; comprehending it, there is fundamentally no swiftness. The Patriarch said, "So it is, so it is."

After a short while, he paid his respects and took his leave. The Patriarch said, "Is your departure too soon? The Master replied, "Since fundamentally there is neither movement nor stillness, how could there be 'soon'?
The Patriarch asked, "Who knows that it is not movement? The Master replied, "It is you, O Benevolent One, who give rise to discrimination.

The Patriarch said, "You have attained a profound state of non-arising. The Master replied, "If there is no arising, how can there be intention? The Patriarch said, "If there is no intention, who gives rise to discrimination? The Master remained silent.
He said, "Discrimination is also not the mind. The Patriarch sighed and said, "Excellent, excellent! Having received this seal of approval, one may finally be called a 'realizer.
How could such a person be compared to those of inferior capacity and weak faculties who claim to have attained what they have not attained, or claim to have realized what they have not realized?
To thoroughly realize this mind is called the Way; to chant and sing of this Way is called song; it flows and spreads throughout the sands of the universe."

This work illuminates future students; it is truly the Tathāgata’s messenger performing the deeds of the Tathāgata. When Yongsheng formerly resided on the stage of study, he derived great benefit from it—what is called:
